#3548. The Out of Touch Adults' Guide to Kid Culture: What Does 'Code Rot' Mean?

A weekly deep dive into the current trends, slang, and viral videos of youth culture in terms that even the squarest can understand.

This week's Out-of-Touch guide takes a look at a phenomena that's probably going to define the lives of generations of young people: Code rot—both actual computer-style code rot, and the more elusive cultural kind. I'm also taking a look at the fake controversy over the "cancellation" of Freddy Krueger, and finally, bringing things home with viral videos of boyfriends dancing.

Expect to hear young people talking about code rot for awhile, maybe for the rest of their lives. It's a concept that's going to affect them more than any previous generation. Code rot, or software rot, describes what happens to a computer program when the hardware and operating system it runs on advance. If older programs aren't updated, they become less stable and glitchy until they eventually become unusable.

The idea of code rot has really caught on in the young people's popular imagination, probably because they're going to spend a lot of their lives dealing with it. They've even taken the idea of code rot into life, and use the phrase to describe anything that is worn out or malfunctioning. If the ice cream machine isn't working at McDonald's, it's code rotted. Bad grades on a report card? Code rot.

Kids are making videos where they demonstrate actual code rot:

or point out physical things that are code rotted, like a cat:

Interestingly, a lot of the online discourse around code rotting concerns the massive video game platform Roblox. Because Roblox games there are made by users, there's often not a lot of incentive for the creators to keep the games current with the platform's changes, so a lot of Gen Z's childhood memories of playing games are sinking into code rot. Here's a video about it:

Another interesting wrinkle is the tone these videos take. Code rot is seen as apocalyptic. While it's mostly hyperbole, I think part of it is the realization that the entire world is code rotted. The old programs that used to run within the "Western Culture" operating system no longer apply and everything is starting to glitch out.

The meaning of "PDF file" depends on the context. If you're at work, it refers to a Portable Document Format file, a format created by Adobe that is famously hard for older people to open. In slang, though, PDF file is algo speak for "pedophile." Because that word is flagged by moderation software online, people say "PDF File" to skirt the censorship.

The run-up to Halloween brought a lot of online discourse about Nightmare on Elm Street villain Freddy Krueger. The supernatural serial murder/PDF File was supposedly cancelled online by overly woke, Gen-Z Tiktokers outraged that he is a child predator. The controversy started with a post from Entertainment Industry Reporter that points out how strange it is that in the '80s and '90s, Freddy Krueger, depicted in 1984's A Nightmare on Elm Street as a child murderer so driven by bloodlust he transcended death, was featured on dolls, board games, and lunchboxes aimed at children. It's a good point, but not a call for "cancellation."

Although the article does say that "Freddy Krueger lunchboxes shouldn’t exist," and that parents "shouldn’t have been buying their kids action figures of a child murderer," this is not a call to action. It's not suggesting cancellation of any kind, and it's hard to even conceive of what cancellation of a fictional character in an old horror franchise would even mean. The article is actually an observation about how merchandising (and low-quality sequels) change the meaning of art. But people online missed the point entirely and invented a scenario where "woke" young people are calling for the cancellations of a fictional villain for doing bad things.

I've been scouring TikTok, looking for even one video where someone is calling for "canceling" Freddy Krueger, and I can't find any, but there are hundreds, maybe thousands of videos like this:

In these videos, people point out how enraging it is that the woke people are calling for Krueger's cancellation and vowing that they won't let it happen. Even though it is not happening. There are even levels to the myths about woke mobs canceling Freddy. Supposedly, younger users were unaware that Krueger is depicted as a "PDF file" as well as a murderer in the 2010 reboot of the franchise, so there are online arguments about whether that's the reason he's being canceled. Even though no one is canceling anything. These anti-woke folks are, ironically, defending a fictional villain from cancellation by creating another fictional villain, the shadowy woke mob that's ruining horror movies. Meanwhile, the real villain is a lack of media literacy. Saying "wow, it's crazy that previous generations made a comedy mascot of such a terrible character and marketed him to children" is not the same as cancellation.

This week's viral videos are of boyfriends dancing. The newest thing on the TikTok is young women sharing video of their boyfriends getting down accompanied by a clip from the song "gay alligations fr. my girlfriend" by TikToker OH MICKEY. Like this:

It's a simple, silly template that maybe doesn't mean a whole lot, but this generation of young men are so messed up when it comes to relationships and masculinity, I'm always happy when a meme becomes popular that indicates that young women want goofy dudes, dudes who know how to dance, and dudes who act silly as boyfriends more than they want red-pilled, manosphere, looksmaxxing types. I don't know if these kinds of messages ever really "break through" to the underground of internet incels, but I like to hope they do, because a lot of young men are not OK.

#3547. The Best Live-Action Sherlock Made The Biggest Change To Arthur Conan Doyle's Character

While there are countless screen versions of Arthur Conan Doyle’s iconic super sleuth, only the BBC’s iconic adaptation of Sherlock Holmes made the change that was needed to redefine the character for a new generation. Without Arthur Conan Doyle’s Sherlock Holmes, viewers would never have gotten the many cop shows and detective dramas that have filled TV listings and streaming services for decades now.

Everything from CBS’s NCIS franchise to True Detective, to Murder She Wrote, to Columbo, to the iconic small-town murder mystery Twin Peaks, all have their shared roots in the author’s iconic mystery stories. Sherlock Holmes was one of the first and most influential heroes of detective fiction, and Conan Doyle’s stories about the character provided many of the formative tropes that still define detective dramas, murder mysteries, and police procedurals to this day.

Despite this, many Sherlock Holmes adaptations have flopped over the decades. Even among the takes on the character that succeeded, almost none could be considered truly definitive takes on the character. While ABC’s Will Trent is the definitive screen version of Karin Slaughter’s novel hero, dozens of different takes on Holmes vie for supremacy. However, the BBC’s adaptation, Sherlock, has one major advantage over the rest of them.

In the past two years alone, Prime Video’s Young Sherlock, The CW’s Sherlock & Daughter, and CBS’s Watson have all, as their titles imply, attempted to find a fresh, original take on the familiar story of Sherlock Holmes. However, none of them have managed to replicate the magic of the BBC’s four-season, 13-episode Sherlock, a live-action version of the character from The League of Gentlemen’s Mark Gatiss and Doctor Who’s Steven Moffat.

Starring Benedict Cumberbatch as Sherlock himself and Martin Freeman as his long-suffering sidekick John Watson, Sherlock made the ingenious decision to move Conan Doyle’s original stories into a contemporary setting. This allowed Sherlock to reintroduce its iconic character as a louche antihero, and saw the BBC show regain some of the edge the original stories boasted during their publication.

While a lot of Sherlock Holmes adaptations lean into the cozy, twee familiarity of the character, much like many Agatha Christie murder mystery shows, it is worth noting that Conan Doyle’s Sherlock Holmes stories weren’t period pieces when they were originally published. The novels were fast-paced thrillers filled with what was then considered cutting edge science, meaning Sherlock’s modern-day setting is arguably truer to the books than a period setting would be.

There is no denying the reality that Sherlock’s final season dropped the proverbial ball and ensured the show didn’t achieve true greatness, but there was still a lot to love in the cult series. As well as making a star of Netflix’s future Tom Ripley, Andrew Scott, in a scene-stealing role as Moriarty, Sherlock provided an updated, thoroughly modern spin on a franchise that had become entirely too staid over the years.

In the years since Sherlock began, there have been innumerable efforts to revive the character for new audiences. 2012’s Elementary, 2018’s Miss Sherlock, the Netflix series The Irregulars, and the upcoming 2027 Sky production The Death of Sherlock Holmes all seek to offer new takes on one of the most iconic characters in literary history, and that’s without even mentioning the trio of hits shows listed above.

Clearly, for all of Sherlock’s flaws, the show’s decision to bring Sherlock into a modern-day setting undeniably injected new life into Conan Doyle’s creation. Imperfect final season or nine, the BBC’s Sherlock proved that Conan Doyle’s Baker Street sleuth was just as urgent and intriguing as ever provided the character got an overdue change of scenery and a new historical era to explore.

Microsoft Visual Studio Professional 2026 is a desktop-only Windows product built as a 64-bit application, designed for people working on real-world codebases. Think multi-project solutions, long build times, and code that’s touched by more than one person. In day-to-day use, the biggest benefit is the context the software provides while you work. #3543. 'The Matrix's Best Line Is Still the Greatest Quote in Franchise History

Though there are many great sci-fi quotes that have been influential in how we view the genre, one line in The Wachowskis’ seminal blockbuster The Matrix has left the biggest mark. The 1999 classic changed the game for how we look at cinema effects, but this line, delivered by Laurence Fishburne to Keanu Reeves, also shows how the movie changed our perception of storytelling. While the film coined some famous phrases that are used to this day, the one that had the most impact is probably the least celebrated.

The line in question comes when Thomas Anderson, aka Neo (Reeves), is retrieved by Trinity (Carrie-Anne Moss) and brought to her leader, Morpheus (Fishburne). Neo sits down with Morpheus, and the latter begins explaining why they are here—because Neo feels a greater truth that he can’t explain, something wrong with the world that feels like “a splinter in your mind.” That feeling can be summed up as “The Matrix,” something that Morpheus describes as a prison that all human beings are born into.

He then leans back with a small case in his hand, and says: “Unfortunately, no one can be told what The Matrix is. You have to see for yourself.” He then offers Neo the famous option of the red and blue pills. Choosing red frees him from The Matrix and awakens him to his reality. Choosing blue allows him to carry on living in the illusion. There are many great lines in movie, but this is perhaps the most impactful, as it defines the nature of the journey all of us are about to take.

It might seem like today, you can find out everything you need to know about a movie from a quick internet search. Trailers, scenes, even the first 10 minutes of a release are routinely shared as part of the marketing. The Matrix was different, with marketing being kept purposefully vague in terms of the storyline to pique viewers’ interest. The infamous first teaser trailer for the film showed a series of unconnected clips without an explanation of the plot, before inviting people to visit www.whatisthematrix.com to gather more clues.

It was a ploy that worked, but even those who ventured into theaters absolutely knowing what The Matrix is were told by this line that it is better to experience it than intellectualize it. On the surface, Morpheus absolutely tells Neo what The Matrix is before saying, “You have to see it for yourself.” The point of the line is that his experience as a character, and ours as a viewer, is better when we see the explanation unfold in front of our eyes. The Matrix is experienced, not debated. It’s lived, not relayed.

The Wachowskis’ work has stood the test of time over a quarter of a century later, and the proof of that influence is in the lines from the movie that have made it into everyday language. The term “red pilled” has made its way into online discourse, while lines such as “free your mind” and “dodge this” have been quoted by fans of the movies ever since. However, Morpheus’ enigmatic quote has the biggest impact, as it sets the viewer up for an experience that, up to that point, was unlike anything else that had been seen in mainstream cinema.

From that moment, we were encouraged to take Neo’s point of view, and leave ourselves open to the adventures of The Matrix. Taking the red pill in that regard meant diving into a timeless spectacle of kung fu, post-apocalyptic sci-fi, and self-liberation. Accepting what came along allowed you to gasp as Neo dodged bullets, leaped from buildings, and defied gravity in one of the greatest climactic fights in cinema history.

There were many imitators that came after The Matrix, films that used the same aesthetics, concepts, and choreography to mimic the pioneering spirit of that 1999 film. However, the original inspiration worked because it refused to be defined by what came before it. The Matrix, both as a concept and as a film, can be written down or explained, but as Morpheus so rightly said, the best way to find out is to see it for yourself.

Bloomberg was the biggest critic, describing it as a “timid” performance that left analysts “sorely disappointed” …

Apple investors and fans hoping to get an insight into the philosophy of new Chief Executive Officer John Ternus on Monday were left sorely disappointed. The 51-year-old’s first earnings call was a timid affair, with Ternus taking cover behind a carefully written script as analysts peppered him with questions.

Newly minted CEO plays it safe during his first high-stakes earnings call? Absolutely shocking! Seriously, what did Bloomberg expect?

Lee acknowledged that the slump in pre-market trading will have been largely driven by Apple’s caution about rising expenses in the current quarter. The company said that memory costs were continuing to rise and that building out Siri AI data centers we’re going to add to the RAM bill. But he argued that Ternus missed an opportunity to talk up the company.

In front of Ternus on Monday night was a chance to counteract the gloom and doom by instilling in Wall Street the fundamentals of the Ternus Doctrine — what he sees Apple becoming under his tenure, the “product guy” taking the company to a new era of innovation. Instead, he spoke like a man glancing at the clock and wishing the minutes away.

Fortune’s Sebastian Herrera was less vocal but echoed some of the criticism.

Ternus fielded some questions but also delegated answers to Chief Financial Officer Kevan Parekh and Chief Operating Officer Sabih Khan, who Apple said would participate in earnings calls moving forward, something the company hasn’t done for years. Ternus projected confidence on the call, but he appeared to stick mostly to scripted marketing points.

It will of course take Ternus some time to develop his own style when it comes to all of the varied aspects of the role, including addressing analysts in earnings calls, but I thought he took a measured but optimistic approach. Given the famously reticent style of his predecessor, the criticism strikes me as rather odd.

#3538. How to Try 'Audio Intelligence' on Your Apple Watch Early

It has been a big year for Apple. There's a new CEO, prices have increased across the board, and there's been a seemingly endless rollout of new devices, including two new Apple Watches: the Series 12 and the Ultra 4. All things considered, these watches offer only minor upgrades over the previous models, shipping with new heart rate monitors and the latest S11 processor. But one of the biggest new watch features, "Audio Intelligence," is also the most controversial—and it's rolling out in beta today.

Audio Intelligence is Apple's branding for a new set of features exclusive to the Series 12 and Ultra 4. These features use the new Apple Watches' hardware, along with on-device and cloud-based AI, for tasks like sound and music identification as well as dictation. "Sound Recognition" can alert you to important sounds, like alarms and doorbells, while "Music Recognition" can automatically display songs playing around you—but these aren't the features you'll hear talked about in discussions of Audio Intelligence.

Rather, everyone is up in arms about "Live Rewind" and "Siri Recap." These Audio Intelligence features passively "listen" to your conversations throughout the day, and, using AI, deliver summaries of what was said. When you double-click your Apple Watch's crown to use Live Rewind, you'll get a loose transcript of the last 15 seconds of conversation it overheard, while Siri Recap can show summaries of all your in-person chats throughout the day. You can even configure a schedule for when your watch is "listening" for recaps—e.g., only run during work hours. Apple suggests each is intended to help jog your memory; maybe you use Siri Recap to remember important discussions you had that morning, while Live Rewind is meant for moments where you forget what someone just said. (As opposed to asking them to repeat themselves, I suppose.)

Apple's claims may or may not assuage your fears, but it seems the company is pushing on ahead regardless. Apple is releasing Audio Intelligence as part of iOS 27.3, which launches in beta on Tuesday. If you have an Apple Watch Series 12 or Ultra 4, you can try it out today, assuming you enroll in Apple's latest beta version.

To do so, you'll need to sign up for the Apple Developer program, since iOS 27.3 is rolling out first for devs. This program used to require a $99 fee, but you can skip it now if you opt for the free account. Once you enroll your Apple Account in this program, you can open your iPhone, head to Settings > General > Software Update > Beta Updates, and choose "iOS 27 Developer Beta." Go back one page, then follow the on-screen instructions to download and install iOS 27.3 when it's available.

#3537. 7 Forgotten Christmas Movies That Deserve to Be Classics

Christmas movies, for some time now, have been an essential part of the holiday season, bringing audiences together with their memorable characters, heartwarming stories, and festive humor. While certain holiday films have become timeless gems that are revisited each year, there are plenty of Christmas masterpieces that have gradually been forgotten about despite being incredibly entertaining and quite meaningful. These forgotten favorites capture the magic of Christmas through their unique stories, emotional moments, and wholesome messages about generosity, love, and togetherness.

Quiet holiday standouts like Christmas with the Kranks, which takes on a hilarious approach to the pressures of the festive season while focusing on a couple whose decision to skip Christmas altogether creates absolute chaos throughout their neighborhood, and the charming romantic comedy Last Holiday, which offers a more uplifting and emotional experience while following a woman who decides to embrace life instead of shying away from it, are just two in the long list of underappreciated Christmas essentials that defiantly deserve a chance to shine during the festive season. Compiled on this list are seven films that stand as mostly forgotten but are worthy enough to be hailed as true classics.

Fred Claus is one of the most cherished Christmas comedies that deserves far more recognition than it's gotten over the years. The holiday classic follows Fred Claus (Vince Vaughn), a man who has grown incredibly cynical after spending most of his life in the shadow of his younger brother Nicholas Claus (Paul Giamatti), whose transformation into Santa turned sibling comparison into a centuries-long grievance.

Fred Claus is as underrated as they come. During its release, the movie received a pretty low rating critically, but most Christmas lovers who have seen it have dubbed it an underappreciated seasonal favorite. One of the film’s biggest highlights is the way it strays away from the generic “save Christmas” trope, instead making it a family film about measuring siblings against one another. Fred Claus is an extremely watchable, indulgent, and oversized film, but a fantastic Christmas classic nonetheless, with enough wholesome moments, holiday charm, and entertaining comedy to make it a forgotten gem that deserves to reign on anyone’s December watchlist.

This 2004 classic film is an extremely entertaining comedy that explores the absolute absurdity of holiday traditions. Christmas with the Kranks centers around Nora (Jamie Lee Curtis) and Luther Krank (Tim Allen) as they both agree that Christmas is simply not worth the expense or aggravation when their daughter Blair (Julie Gonzalo) leaves home for a Peace Corps assignment.

Christmas with the Kranks expertly turns familiar seasonal pressures into exaggerated comedy. Few comedies in the genre come close to illustrating the gap between the opinions of professional critics and viewers’ enjoyment of festive entertainment. Upon its release, Christmas with the Kranks wasn’t received well by critics, leading it to go mostly unnoticed by mainstream viewers. Despite its underrated status, what makes it such an enjoyable film is how its exaggerated humor eventually leads to a genuinely heartening celebration of community. Christmas with the Kranks stands as a relatable bout of Christmas entertainment, as it delivers those recognizable holiday frustrations and a sentimental conclusion.

Just Friends is definitely not the first movie that comes to most people’s minds when thinking of extraordinary Christmas classics, but its hilarious romantic complications and holiday setting make it a strong contender for this list of underrated gems. The film focuses on Chris Brander (Ryan Reynolds), who, as a teen, was socially awkward, overweight, insecure, and completely in love with his best friend, who broke his heart by insisting they remain “just friends.” Years pass, and Chris has reinvented himself, but unfortunately for him, his visit back home and the presence of his childhood crush bring back all of his adolescent insecurity.

Sure, Just Friends may be marketed simply as a mid-2000s Ryan Reynolds comedy rather than as a true Christmas staple, but it deserves its credit for being an enduring comedy that is honestly pretty perfect for a seasonal watch. The film’s premise works because of Christmas; it’s a returning-home-for-the-holidays bout of fun that blends nicely with other well-known tropes that keep the movie interesting. From the snow and family embarrassment to the decorations and romantic nostalgia, Just Friends makes for a truly captivating and rewatchable early-2000s Christmas classic.

This often overlooked film is an unconventional Christmas classic that avoids the usual holiday cheer and comfort. Set on Christmas Eve, Better Watch Out centers around Ashley (Olivia DeJonge), who arrives at a suburban house to babysit 12-year-old Luke Lerner (Levi Miller).

Better Watch Out isn’t the type of film that needs to be a detailed recommendation, as revealing too much about the movie can severely damage the viewing experience. Because of this, the film stands far apart from the well-known mainstream Christmas watches that audiences usually revisit during the season. Better Watch Out doesn’t rely on warmth and cheer; instead, the movie takes on a much darker approach, using a seemingly innocent premise to deliver quite the unsettling experience. It’s a truly captivating film that may not be the usual, spirited good time, but stands as an unconventional classic for the festive season.

Unaccompanied Minors is a woefully underrated Christmas classic that most who have seen it have likely dubbed it a fever dream. With a Christmas Eve blizzard stranding hundreds of travelers at an airport, the 2006 film follows a group of children traveling without their parents as they turn the large travel hub into a playground for increasingly elaborate schemes, rebellion, and friendships.

Unaccompanied Minors deserves far more attention than it has received for its ability to turn an ordinary holiday travel disaster into such an entertaining adventure. The movie effortlessly combines genuine Christmas spirit with childhood mischief. With an energetic young cast to keep things hilarious and captivatingly wholesome, Unaccompanied Minors is a terribly overlooked film that wields enough personality and entertainment to be labeled an undeniable holiday classic.

This underrated Christmas gem is the holiday romance that everyone should place on their December watchlist. Last Holiday centers on the reserved Georgia Byrd (Queen Latifah), who mistakenly believes she has only a short time left to live. With that in mind, Georgia chooses to spend her supposed time left traveling and living with less fear.

Last Holiday is one of those uplifting tales that truly deserves to be considered a Christmas classic because it offers the perfect cocktail of discovering happiness, learning to leap without fear, and embracing opportunities with open arms. The film is actually remembered quite fondly by many viewers but is still shoved under the long and brilliant list of Queen Latifah’s romantic comedies instead of being placed on Christmas watch essentials. Last Holiday is genuinely perfect for those searching for a Christmas film that doesn’t revolve around traditional themes of the holiday or Santa Claus, making it a unique, feel-good gem.

The Preacher’s Wife is a woefully underappreciated Christmas classic that deserves to be among all these Christmas essentials because of its ability to capture the warmth of community and the true spirit of the holiday. The film focuses on a minister's family struggling with financial difficulties, pressures of maintaining their congregation, and personal frustrations, as they unexpectedly find the answers to their prayers at the arrival of an angel tasked with helping them.

The Preacher’s Wife isn’t a movie that can completely fade into the ether, because there is always someone lingering somewhere who has devoted their time to praising the film, especially among Whitney Houston fans. Unfortunately, despite its star-studded cast, the movie still doesn’t get the attention it deserves. The Preacher’s Wife wields the captivating emotional power of music and stands as a worthy classic due to how seamlessly it blends uplifting storytelling with its musical talent, making it a great addition to this list of Christmas hits.

#3536. New iPad mini hands-on: Refreshed design, OLED display, more

Apple’s smallest iPad has gotten its biggest update in years. The new iPad mini features a much thinner and lighter design, a larger OLED display, water resistance, and the powerful A20 Pro chip.

I’ve been testing the new iPad mini, and there’s a lot to like — but also a couple of frustrations. Here’s everything you need to know.

The new iPad mini lives up to the “mini” name even more than its predecessor. It’s significantly thinner, down from 6.3mm on the previous iPad mini to 5.4mm on the new model. In fact, that puts it very close to the ultra-thin iPad Pro and the unfolded iPhone Duo. Here’s how it compares:

The new iPad mini is also significantly lighter, dropping from 293 grams to 255 grams. That puts it in the realm of the iPhone Duo, for comparison’s sake:

The reduction in weight and thickness was immediately noticeable when I picked up the new iPad mini. It feels significantly nicer to hold, more premium, and less “dense” in my hands.

The new iPad mini features an 8.5-inch screen, a slight increase from the previous generation’s 8.3-inch display. The overall footprint is mostly the same (the new model is actually about 2.2mm narrower). The larger screen is possible because the new iPad mini’s bezels are 24 percent thinner than before.

In addition to allowing a bigger screen in the same form factor, the narrower bezels also modernize the iPad mini’s overall look and feel. The bezels are noticeably slimmer than the iPad Air and base model iPad, and slightly thinner than the iPad Pro.

With smaller bezels, a thinner chassis, and a lighter weight, the new iPad mini feels significantly more premium than before. It reminds me less of the base model iPad or iPad Air and more of the iPad Pro, just shrunken down.

The big news about the display, though, is the switch to OLED. This marks Apple’s first non-Pro iPad to offer an OLED screen. It’s not the fancy tandem OLED display of the iPad Pro, but it’s a huge improvement over the previous model’s LCD panel.

The new iPad mini offers SDR brightness up to 600 nits, up from the previous model’s 500 nits max. The iPad mini also supports HDR content, with up to 1200 nits peak brightness.

The new iPad mini’s screen is undeniably an improvement over its predecessor. All of the inherent benefits of OLED apply here, including better colors, improved contrast, higher brightness, and more.

Unfortunately, the new iPad mini’s screen has one limitation: it doesn’t support ProMotion, or a 120Hz refresh rate of any kind. Instead, it’s still locked to 60Hz. This is an incredibly frustrating decision that I can’t quite wrap my head around.

Apple touts the iPad mini’s OLED screen as offering significantly faster pixel response time than the previous generation’s LCD panel, leading to improvements like smoother scrolling and reduced motion blur.

I’ve noticed that things like swiping between Home Screen pages, scrolling social media, and system animations are noticeably smoother. They aren’t, however, as smooth as an Apple device with a ProMotion display, and they’re not a substitute for a higher refresh-rate display.

I’m sure Apple knows the iPad mini’s market, and it seems to have decided not to prioritize ProMotion based on that information. However, as someone who has longed for a so-called “iPad mini Pro” for years, I’m disappointed by the decision. The new iPad mini’s screen is so much better … I just wish Apple had gone that extra step and added ProMotion. We’ve reached a point where ProMotion should be table stakes, especially after Apple brought it to the base iPhone 17 last year.

For an extra $100, you can upgrade the new iPad mini to have a nano-texture display (on the 256GB and 512GB models).

I’m a huge fan of Apple’s nano-texture display and have it on my 14-inch MacBook Pro. On the iPad mini, I think it makes even more sense.

The iPad mini is ultra-portable, and you naturally carry it around and use it in different lighting environments. The nano-texture glass helps reduce reflections and glare in a wide variety of lighting conditions. I also really like the combination of the iPad mini’s book-like size and the nano-texture finish.

There is a slight tradeoff in color vibrancy compared to a glossy OLED screen, as on other Apple devices with nano-texture, but it’s a very minor difference in my experience. The screen still looks fantastic.

One of the more interesting changes with the new iPad mini is something Apple calls the “Acoustic Display.” Instead of traditional speakers with visible grilles, Apple has developed a new system that uses the display itself to produce sound.

Essentially, Apple has designed special woofers that vibrate the display to produce low and midrange frequencies. For higher frequencies, custom tweeters are hidden between the glass and aluminum enclosure. Apple says this new system delivers louder audio, “punchier” bass, and clearer highs, despite the iPad mini’s significantly thinner design.

In practice, I think the new iPad mini sounds great. I’d choose headphones or an external speaker for serious music or video consumption, but day-to-day the iPad mini’s built-in speakers are perfectly adequate. (I’d bet that this Acoustic Display technology shows up in future iPhones too, and the iPad mini is serving as a test bed of sorts.)

The Acoustic Display also plays an important role in another major upgrade: water and dust resistance. The new iPad mini is IP67 rated, which means it can be immersed in 1 meter of freshwater for up to 30 minutes. It’s the first iPad to have an official water-resistance rating.

Adding water resistance to the iPad mini is particularly notable given its size and portability. I naturally find myself wanting to take it everywhere, and water resistance makes that more feasible.

One use case where all these improvements really come together is reading. The thinner and lighter design, nano-texture glass, and water resistance make the new iPad mini the most compelling iPad yet to serve as an e-reader.

The new iPad mini is powered by Apple’s A20 Pro chip, which I already covered in detail in my iPhone 18 Pro review. The short version: the A20 Pro chip gives you plenty of power for anything you can throw at the iPad mini today.

One detail worth calling out is that Apple uses two different versions of the A20 Pro in the iPad mini. The 128GB and 256GB models feature a five-core CPU and 16-core Neural Engine, while the 512GB model gets a six-core CPU and Dual 16-core Neural Engine. All three configurations feature the same seven-core GPU.

I don’t think anyone should buy the 512GB version of the iPad mini just for those extra cores. You should pick your iPad mini configuration based on how much storage you need, not the version of the A20 Pro chip. You don’t need to worry about performance with the new iPad mini. And perhaps most importantly, the A20 Pro chip ensures the iPad mini has enough headroom for the future.

There’s been a lot of consternation about where the iPad mini fits in a world where the iPhone Duo also now exists. It’s a fair question. After all, when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, the two devices share a similar form factor … but that’s really where the similarities end.

The iPad mini offers the full-fledged, unapologetic iPadOS experience. It supports the full multitasking prowess of an iPad Pro, including windowing and the menu bar. The new iPad mini also supports extended display mode, so you can plug it into an external display and extend your iPad experience there.

The iPad mini also gets iPadOS app layouts, and most importantly, a desktop-class browsing experience in Safari. It’s a remarkably capable device in a remarkably compact form factor. It fits where other iPads can’t, yet it runs the same version of iPadOS as other iPads.

The new iPad mini does all of that, but better than before. The thinner, lighter design paired with smaller bezels gives the new iPad mini a meaningful visual refresh. The added water resistance means you can do even more with the compact and pocketable iPad mini design.

But all of this comes at a higher price of $699. This marks the second price increase for the iPad mini this year. It started the year at $499, rose to $599 as part of Apple’s broader price increases in June, and is now $699 as of this refresh.

The new iPad mini also still starts with 128GB of storage. Increasing the base storage to 256GB would’ve helped ease some of the pain of that price increase. It’s also getting increasingly hard to manage a device with 128GB, particularly with the storage needs of Apple Intelligence and Siri AI. The lack of ProMotion and Face ID also make the price increase sting more.

Ultimately, the iPad mini form factor is a joy to use. The design feels great in the hand, and having the full iPadOS experience in such a compact device remains impressive. It’s not quite the “iPad mini Pro” I’ve always wanted, but it’s big upgrade to a form factor that I’ve always loved.

#3535. Amazon Fire TV Stick HD Review: Small, speedy, and easy on the wallet

The Amazon Fire TV Stick HD is a simple, affordable way to make a 1080p TV smarter. The new Vega OS feels quick, its slimmer design can run straight off your TV's USB port, and setup is a breeze. It's limited to 1080p and can't sideload apps like Fire OS, so if you own a 4K TV, you should spend a bit more on the new Amazon Fire Stick 4K.

Responsive, easy-to-use interface with new Vega OS

Slim design that runs off your TV's USB port

No third-party app sideloading like Fire OS

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Streaming sticks don't need to be fancy to hit their mark, and the Amazon Fire TV Stick HD is a great reminder of that. If you've got an older TV that's still going strong but has sluggish smart features (or perhaps none at all), a $35 streaming stick is an easy fix.

The 2026 Fire TV Stick HD runs Vega OS, Amazon's Linux-based software, which replaces the Android-based Fire OS that powered previous models. Amazon says the changes make it more than 30 percent faster, and it also brings a slimmer body, USB power, Wi-Fi 6 support, and free Alexa+.

It's not all pros across the board. The resolution caps out at 1080p, you can't sideload third-party apps anymore, and there's no support for Dolby Vision. But if you're shopping for a bedroom, guest room, or an older TV set that you don't primarily use, the Fire TV Stick HD is one of the cheaper streaming devices you should take a closer look at.

The Amazon Fire TV Stick HD launched on April 29, 2026, for $34.99, which is the same price as the 2024 model it replaced. It's Amazon's cheapest streaming stick, and it sits below the Fire TV Stick 4K and the Fire TV Stick 4K Max. Amazon ran a limited-time deal that brought the stick down to $21.99 shortly after launch, so we'll likely see temporary price cuts around the holiday shopping season.

Keep in mind that the stick's new "Direct Power" feature means that it gets power right from your TV's USB port. If your TV doesn't have a USB port, you'll need to pick up an adapter separately.

The Fire TV Stick HD is about as minimal as a streaming device gets, and Amazon says it's the slimmest Fire TV device the company has made. That makes it really easy to tuck behind a TV or toss in a bag for a trip, and it won't crowd the other ports and cables on your set.

The only other connection is a USB-C port for power, and thanks to "Direct Power," you can plug it straight into your TV's USB port with the included cable. That means you'll have one less wall adapter to hide, and your setup will look a lot cleaner as a result.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The included Alexa Voice Remote covers all the basics, including voice search, menu navigation, TV power, and volume controls. It doesn't have fancy extras like a remote finder or backlit buttons, but it gets the job done. (If you want Amazon's redesigned Fire TV remote, which I liked a lot more, you'll have to get the Fire TV Stick 4K.)

Setup is about as easy as it gets. Just plug the stick into your TV's HDMI port, connect the USB-C cable to your TV's USB port, and follow the on-screen prompts. You'll then have to connect to Wi-Fi and sign in with your Amazon account, and you're off to the races.

Since Vega OS only lets you install apps from the Amazon app store, you should make sure that the ones you use most are actually available. Netflix, YouTube, Disney+, Prime Video, Hulu, and other popular streaming services all run natively, but niche apps may be missing due to the lack of third-party app sideloading, which the older Fire OS allowed you to do.

The Fire TV Stick HD has a quad-core 1.7GHz processor and 8GB of storage. It can stream up to 1080p resolution with HDR10, HDR10+, and HLG, and it supports Dolby Atmos through HDMI pass-through if you have a compatible sound setup. There's no Dolby Vision here, and it won't output 4K, so it's really only meant for 1080p TV sets.

Vega OS keeps menus and home screen rows moving smoothly, and apps open quickly. I didn't have any issues switching between my most used apps on the fly. Amazon's "30 percent faster" figure is its own claim, so I wouldn't treat it as fact, but it definitely felt faster than my past Fire OS experiences.

I also like that the Fire TV Stick HD isn't limited to video. You can pair a Bluetooth game controller and play cloud games through Amazon Luna or Xbox Game Pass, which is a fun bonus, and you can even connect a pair of headphones for late-night viewing. It comes with Alexa+ free of charge, which can come in handy when you're trying to hunt down something new to watch.

The downsides are pretty familiar to past Fire TV Sticks. A big chunk of the Fire TV home screen is taken up by recommendations and sponsored content, and you'll definitely notice it (especially if you're used to Roku's cleaner layout like I am).

Sideloading third-party apps is also gone, which will bug those who liked using older Fire TV Sticks for apps that aren't available in Amazon's app store. Neither is a dealbreaker for the average viewer, but they're worth knowing about before diving in.

The Amazon Fire TV Stick HD is a fast, simple, and affordable streaming stick that's a perfect match for older HD TVs and secondary rooms. Vega OS feels speedy, the slim design and USB power keep things neat, and setup takes just a few minutes. You won't get 4K streaming resolution, Dolby Vision, or third-party app sideloading, but for $34.99 (or less on sale), it's hard to complain.

If you're looking for an alternative pick, the base model Roku Streaming Stick ($39) also tops out at 1080p, but has a cleaner interface.

In Amazon’s ecosystem, the new Fire TV Stick 4K costs $25 more, but you get 4K resolution output and a redesigned (and much better) remote. And if you're a tinkerer who wants to sideload apps, the Fire TV Stick 4K Max is the only Amazon stick that still runs Android-based Fire OS.

If you've got an older 1080p TV and want a cheap way to get streaming apps on it, the Fire TV Stick HD is a solid choice that won't break the bank.

#3534. Mickey’s Surprising Incompetence Balances Sheriff Country’s Excellence In Season 2

Cher Thompson is a Senior Staff Writer at Screen Rant, where she covers everything from explosive reality TV moments to cast interviews about the twists and turns of scripted dramas. With a background in creative writing, marketing, and teaching, Cher knows how to spot both the storytelling genius and the guilty pleasures in pop culture. Her work blends wit with insight, making readers feel like they’re chatting with a friend who just happens to know way too much about TV.

Despite Sheriff Mickey Fox (Morena Baccarin) often being good at her job, Sheriff Country season 2's crossover event made it clear that, even through a fantastic season, she can still have some level of incompetence. Throughout the run of the CBS spinoff, which just aired its first crossover event of the season with Fire Country, viewers have gotten the chance to see Mickey find her footing as Edgewater's sheriff. While Mickey dealt with difficulties in her personal and professional life, she's been able to prove herself throughout the show's run with good reads on both cases and those close to her.

While there's no doubt that Mickey is great at her job, it's been interesting to see her move through the issues in Edgewater throughout the early episodes of Sheriff Country season 2, especially as the show has thrown more in her way when it comes to her personal life. After mixing business and family throughout the first stretch of the season when Mickey's formerly presumed dead mother, DEA agent Eva Santos (Rachel Ticotin), was brought into the mix for a tough case, Mickey's judgment has been clouded more than once.

While her father, Wes Fox (W. Earl Brown), has always been making her life difficult, Mickey's had a difficult go of things this season, which has made it all the more interesting to watch her navigate her professional responsibilities. During Sheriff Country season 2 episode 5, "No Way In," Mickey's ability to remain professional was put to the test, and wavered more than it has in the past.

Although Mickey has long had to balance the difficulties of being a parent to her daughter, Skye (Amanda Arcuri), and handling the demanding side of her duties around Edgewater, the most recent episode of Sheriff Country saw her struggling to separate the professional and the personal. While Mickey did the noble thing jumping in to take Skye's place when she was being held hostage by a criminal who was out for the sheriff after a prison break, knowing she did it out of a personal risk as Skye's mother rather than a professional standpoint made it a tough decision to support.

Throughout the episode of Sheriff Country, it was clear that Mickey struggled to separate the nerves she was feeling about Skye being trapped at The Meat Up with a dangerous group of criminals from the ways she was handling the issue. While it was risky regardless of whether Skye was there or not, the fact that Mickey had to contend with her feelings as a mother made her feel more human in some regards, and threw her off her game entirely in others. It was clear that having Skye at risk was more difficult for the sheriff than anything she's faced before.

While Sheriff Country does a great job at showing Mickey balancing everything in her life well, the series needs to move on from the trope that's defined her character since the beginning of the series. Mickey is a complicated woman who deals with far more than most, but the fact that we as viewers rarely see her struggling with her decisions, emotions, or the realities of her life isn't a net positive. It's great that she can handle herself, but watching Mickey compartmentalize and vent her feelings, often to her sister Sharon Leone (Diane Farr) over a glass of wine, is growing tired.

Sheriff Country has allowed Mickey to be complicated enough of a character to support the fact that she may not always have everything together, and she definitely doesn't always know the right answers. Unfortunately, the show often makes it seem like Mickey is readily able to handle everything thrown at her, even if it's exhausting. Seeing her crack in some ways, even as she volunteered to allow a known criminal interested in killing her to take her hostage, was a refreshing shift for the series. Sheriff Country would be better to let Mickey continue to struggle, as it will make her rebounding all the more interesting.

#3532. Apple explains the $400 premium for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display

Apple argued that the touchscreen isn’t the headline feature of the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display, merely a bonus.

The headline should instead be the quality of the display itself – with the company effectively suggesting that the $400 premium is positively cheap for what you’re getting …

Apple published a white paper in which it argues that the latest MacBook Pro display is essentially a smaller version of its professional reference monitor, the Studio Display XDR.

$400 for the screen and new design isn’t my issue, my issue is the cost of storage and memory. $600 more to go from 24gb to 48gb or nearly a grand for 64gb. You can easily spend nearly double the cost of the machine just getting it to a semi-future proof spec.

Given that this costs anywhere from $2,899 to $3,599 just for a display (albeit a significantly larger one with a correspondingly higher resolution), this does put into perspective that $400 extra over the MacBook Pro with the standard screen. Here’s what Apple has to say about it:

PROLED XDR display, the best display in a pro laptop, finally overcomes these historic limitations. For the first time, a MacBook Pro display uses tandem OLED technology, delivering up to 1000 nits of sustained full-screen brightness, 2000 nits of peak high dynamic range (HDR) and standard dynamic range (SDR) brightness, and a 10,000,000:1 contrast ratio with accurate, per-pixel black levels.

It’s driven in real time by an all-new display engine in M5 Pro and M5 Max, which continuously compensates each pixel for content, usage, temperature, and ambient conditions—delivering creative precision out of the box and protecting panel lifespan over time. And a unique manufacturing process ensures panel-to-panel consistency and minimizes off-axis color shift, a first for any OLED laptop.

As Macworld spotted, that’s almost identical to the company’s description of the the Studio Display XDR.

In fact, the PROLED XDR in the MacBook Pro is the only display other than the Studio Display XDR that supports Apple CMF 2026, the next generation of CIE 1931. Apple says CMF 2026 “more precisely aligns the appearance of the display with an ideal D65 illuminant—the standard reference for white—and significantly improves appearance matching across display technologies, which is important for workflows that use multiple displays side by side.”

Resolution aside, the other specs are identical with just one exception: the contrast ratio. As for that exception, the MacBook display comes out on top with a 10 million to 1 contrast ratio, in contrast with the Studio Display XDR’s one million.

Does this change your own perspective of the price premium of the OLED model? Please share your thoughts in the comments.

#3531. Taylor Sheridan’s Original Western Masterpiece Officially Named Paramount+'s Biggest 2026 Hit

2026 has been another busy year for Taylor Sheridan, but that isn’t that surprising to those who have been following his work for the last 10 years. As much impact as Sheridan has in the movie and TV landscape, you’d think he’d been around much longer than 10 years, but he made his feature writing debut only 11 years ago on one of the best neo-Western crime thrillers ever made, Sicario. Sheridan also penned the script for the Sicario sequel that was released in 2018, but he isn’t returning for the third Sicario movie that was just announced a few weeks ago. Steven Knight, the Peaky Blinders scribe who is also writing the next James Bond movie, is penning the script for Sicario 3, so even with Sheridan’s departure, it’s safe to say the movie is in good hands.

Fans could argue that movies like Sicario or even Wind River are what Sheridan is best known for, but the TV show that put him on the map was Yellowstone. Starring Kevin Costner, Sheridan released five seasons of Yellowstone between its premiere in 2018 and its conclusion in 2024, but the show lives on as one of the most-watched projects in the world on streaming. In America, Yellowstone is Sheridan’s only show that streams on Peacock, but it’s still one of the most-watched titles in the world on Paramount Plus globally, where it’s been in the top 10 for over 300 days this year. This is an elite streaming milestone known only to a select few movies and shows, but it’s not surprising that Sheridan’s most popular show ever is still outlasting newer competitors on watchlists.

The show that claimed the most of your answers is the world you were built for. If two tied, both are shown — you're complicated enough to straddle two Sheridan universes.

You are a Dutton — or you might as well be. You understand that some things are worth protecting at any cost, and that the modern world's indifference to history, to land, to legacy, is not something you're willing to accept quietly. You lead from the front, you carry your family's weight without complaint, and when someone threatens what's yours, you don't escalate — you finish it. You're not cruel. But you are absolute. In Yellowstone's world, that combination of ferocity and loyalty doesn't make you a villain. It makes you the only thing standing between everything that matters and everyone who wants to take it.

You thrive in the chaos of high-stakes negotiation, where the money is enormous, the margins are thin, and the wrong word in the wrong room can cost everyone everything. You're a fixer — the person called when a situation is already on fire and needs someone with the nerve to walk into it. West Texas oil country rewards exactly what you are: sharp, adaptable, unsentimental, and absolutely clear-eyed about what people want and what they'll do to get it. You're not naive enough to think this world is fair. You're smart enough to be the one deciding who it's fair to.

You are a Dwight Manfredi — someone who has served their time, paid their dues, and arrived somewhere unexpected with nothing but their reputation and their wits. You adapt without losing yourself. You build loyalty through respect rather than fear, though you're not above reminding people that the two aren't mutually exclusive. Tulsa King is for people who are still standing when everyone assumed they'd be finished — who find, in an unfamiliar place, that they're more capable than the world gave them credit for. You don't need a throne. You build one, wherever you happen to land.

You carry the weight of a system that is broken by design, and you do it anyway — because someone has to, and because you're the only one positioned to do it without the whole thing collapsing. Mike McLusky's world is for people who are comfortable operating where there are no good options, only less catastrophic ones. You speak every language: law enforcement, criminal, political, human. That fluency makes you invaluable and it makes you a target. You've made your peace with both. Mayor of Kingstown belongs to people who understand that keeping the peace is not the same as being at peace — and who do the job regardless.

The original Yellowstone show may be over, but the story of the Duttons is far from over. Earlier this year, Paramount released two new Yellowstone spin-offs, Marshals and Dutton Ranch. The former follows Luke Grimes’ Kayce Dutton now that he’s left ranch life behind for a life in law enforcement, and the latter centers around Cole Hauser’s Rip Wheeler and Kelly Reilly’s Beth Dutton. Marshals is already back for Season 2, with new episodes releasing weekly on CBS, and Dutton Ranch is expected to return for Season 2 next year.

Check out all five seasons of Yellowstone on Peacock in America or on Paramount+ globally and stay tuned to Collider for more updates and coverage of Taylor Sheridan’s future projects.

In an interview with the Happy Sad Confused podcast, Bill Skarsgård opened up about his history portraying some iconic villains, including Count Orlok in Nosferatu and Pennywise the Dancing Clown in the IT franchise. When discussing the fan casts and hopes for the actor to join the Bond franchise and portray another villain, Skarsgård stated:

"It would have to be something that felt original to me, that was something that I hadn’t done before. I feel, kind of, spent with those things. #3526. Pokémon Legends: Z-A Freebie Officially Available Until November 18

Pokémon Legends: Z-A, like its predecessors, has continued to be supported long after launch with special distributions and limited-time events. This constant stream of updates ensures that returning players have something new and exciting awaiting them in Lumiose City, and new players have even more reasons to stick around. While they'll eventually stop, for now, the assorted freebies, downloads, and events are a fun bonus that helps make Legends: Z-A feel that little bit more worthwhile.

There are numerous ongoing Pokémon Legends: Z-A events that players can take part in, but the one they'll absolutely want to pay attention to is a free download that can only be claimed before November 18. This is absolutely worth claiming if you're a fan of the game or are looking for even more Pokémon to add to your collection, especially as it could result in gaining a rare pattern. You'll need to be quick, of course, but fortunately, so long as you have a copy of the game, it's very easy to obtain.

Right now, players can claim a free Mystery Gift in Pokémon Legends: Z-A. This is Game Freak's way of distributing Pokémon or various items to all players, something it does on a fairly frequent basis. The Mystery Gift this time is Spewpa, a Bug-type Pokémon originally introduced back in Gen 6. Spewpa can be caught in the base game or evolved from Scatterbug at level 9, but this Mystery Gift cuts out the need to hunt one down and simply adds it to your collection.

In order to get the Mystery Gift, you'll need to first head to the main menu and select Link Play. From there, just select Mystery Gift, and then "Get via Internet." Once you've done that, Spewpa will be added to your account, allowing you to add it to your party and evolve it. You don't need a Nintendo Online subscription, despite the fact that you need an internet connection in order to get it. Additionally, you can only get one per save file, and the account playing must be tied to a registered Nintendo Account.

Once you have Spewpa, you'll be able to evolve it at level 12 into a Vivillon, which can have one of 16 unique patterns. There is no way of guaranteeing that the Spewpa obtained via the Mystery Gift will have a certain pattern, so you'll need to hope that you get the one you want. Of course, if you don't, you can simply head back into Wild Zone 4 during the day to find one in the wild. Alternatively, Spewpa's can be located near trees and in grassy areas all across Lumiose City.

This Mystery Gift in Pokémon Legends: Z-A is only available until November 18 at 9 pm ET. While it doesn't quite make up for a lack of a brand-new Pokémon Legends game, it should hopefully give Z-A fans something new to entertain themselves with for a short while. At the very least, it gives Spewpa fans another win, and those hunting down every variant of Vivillon in Pokémon Legends: Z-A the opportunity to complete their collection.

#3525. John Ternus talks plans to improve Siri AI

During Apple’s quarterly earnings call, CEO John Ternus was asked repeatedly about Siri AI’s future. Here’s what he said about Apple’s plans for improving and expanding Siri AI.

Sometimes when Apple launches a new feature or product, the company sees its work as finished, and whatever ships goes unchanged for far too long. Many might characterize Siri this way, arguing the assistant went years without meaningful improvement or updates.

But according to Apple CEO John Ternus, the Siri AI that just shipped is only the beginning of what’s planned.

Yesterday on Apple’s quarterly earnings call, Ternus gave a rundown of Siri AI’s capabilities. He concluded: “We’re really excited to have rolled all these innovations out, and there’s still so much more we plan to do.”

This signals that Apple doesn’t see Siri AI as a feature that can now be left alone for a while. Instead, as we already saw in iOS 27.2 last week, Apple is focused on rapidly improving it.

Now that Siri AI is out, I would like to see it iterate as follows:

Support for a wider range of file types, such as PDF.

Accessing it from Search (especially on the Mac) should be instantaneous and reliable.

Proactively suggesting and reminding the user based on what it knows.

What are those future plans? It sounds like agentic capabilities may be among them. Ternus said:

With Siri AI, we really have the kind of—the Siri we always wanted. It’s primarily request-based today, but as we talked about at WWDC, it’s built on a modern, orchestrator-driven architecture that gives us real room to expand capabilities over time.

It’s telling that Ternus says Siri is “primarily request-based today” and mentions “room to expand capabilities” before pivoting to mention agentic features. It sounds like Apple is already, behind-the-scenes, envisioning and working toward a version of Siri that won’t need to be “primarily request-based.”

Finally, later in the call when discussing opportunities for services growth, including potentially launching new services, Ternus says: “We think intelligence is going to be another opportunity as well.” This refers back to an earlier discussion of Apple’s intent to charge a fee for expanded usage limits on certain Siri AI and Apple Intelligence capabilities. The idea is that as Siri evolves and improves, Apple will have opportunities to charge for certain features.

What are your takeaways from Ternus’s comments on Siri AI? Let us know in the comments.

#3522. New 4-Part Crime Thriller Officially Arrives on Netflix

The best crime dramas can keep audiences guessing about who committed a murder. But the truly elite? They're better off when they tell us what happens when it seems like the investigation is over. While shows like Mindhunter and True Detective have built enormous followings by exploring the darker corners of criminal investigations, one of the most critically acclaimed dramas of the 2010s took a much quieter approach. And despite earning the sort of reviews most television creators could only dream of, it somehow managed to remain relatively overlooked. Until now, perhaps.

All four seasons of Rectify have officially arrived on Netflix in the United States, joining the streaming service on November 1. The acclaimed drama originally aired on SundanceTV between 2013 and 2016, producing 30 episodes and earning widespread critical acclaim throughout its run, even winning one of the most prestigious awards going.

When Daniel Holden is released after nearly 20 years of complete isolation on Death Row, he returns as an outsider to his family, to his community, and to the times. Somehow, he survived the mental and emotional strain of his imprisonment, but now the walls have suddenly come crumbling down, and Daniel is set free in a world he no longer understands. He’s an outsider, lost in a once familiar world, struggling to navigate his newfound freedom. Combined with two decades of technological and social changes to his small town and the larger world, everything he encounters is a puzzle.

The cast stars Aden Young (The King Tide) as Daniel Holden, Abigail Spencer (Timeless) as Amantha Holden, Adelaide Clemens (Silent Hill: Revelation) as Tawney Talbot, Clayne Crawford (Lethal Weapon) as Ted Talbot Jr., J. Smith-Cameron (Succession) as Janet Talbot, Bruce McKinnon (Lawless) as Ted Talbot Sr., Luke Kirby (The Marvelous Mrs. Maisel) as Jon Stern, and Sean Bridgers (Get Shorty) as Trey Willis. The show is created by Ray McKinnon (Deadwood).

Rectify was met with universal acclaim from critics and audiences, receiving a score of 96% on Rotten Tomatoes, with the audience score not far behind at 92%. Its third and fourth seasons both earned perfect 100% critics' scores, while the final season achieved an extraordinary 99 out of 100 on Metacritic; it also received a coveted Peabody Award, which shows just how highly regarded it was.

All 30 episodes of Rectify, spanning four seasons, are streaming now on Netflix in the United States.

#3521. PlayStation Plus Makes 10/10 Turn-Based Sci-Fi RPG Completely Free

If you have a PlayStation Plus Premium subscription, you may care to know that one of the very best RPGs of the PS2 generation is currently free with the subscription service. Better yet, it still completely holds up in 2026. Don't believe me? Go play it for yourself and out.

When it comes to PS2 RPGs, the bar is pretty damn high. Dragon Quest VIII: Journey of the Cursed King is still a complete masterpiece. Then there are some of the best Final Fantasy games ever made on the console. Of course, Square Enix aren't the only studio that makes RPGs, and there's one turn-based PS2 game that has never really had the love it deserves.

The PlayStation Plus library of PS1 and PS2 games isn't what it should be given how much a PlayStation Plus Premium subscription costs, but there are still some great games to be found there. One such game is the wonderful Rogue Galaxy. Developed by Level-5 (Ni no Kuni, Professor Layton), this 2005 sci-fi RPG remains, to my mind, a genuine 10/10 masterpiece. It's also managed to age beautifully, which is a rare feat for games of that era.

A big part of how the game managed to age so well should come as little surprise: the wonderful, timeless cel-shaded art style. Much like The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker, Rogue Galaxy's decision to go for a cartoon aesthetic over something more realistic has ensured it still looks incredible today. Its huge galaxy, which is made up of multiple planets, also remains a delight to explore.

Rogue Galaxy also delivers an epic tale with a wonderful cast of characters, which tends to be key for any good RPG. It wears its Star Wars influences on its sleeve, too. The game begins with a young farmer who becomes entangled in a galactic conflict, and ultimately becomes responsible for the fate of the cosmos. Definitely seen that somewhere before.

If you're looking for a sci-fi RPG that offers more fantasy elements, Rogue Galaxy is one of the best choices out there. It's much, much less serious and gritty than something like Mass Effect, but still able to deliver an emotional punch when it has to.

The only real thing to remember is that this is a two-decade-old game, and even while it's largely aged well, there are some rough edges. If you can roll with those punches, though, you'll get a brilliant 40-hour adventure in return. Not bad at all, right?

#3520. iOS 27.2 adds two new features I’ve been really loving

iOS 27.2 arrived last week with a variety of new features and changes for iPhone. Here are two new iOS 27.2 features I’ve been loving lately.

I’ve used Apple Podcasts for the last few years after previously sticking with third-party apps. The native Podcasts app won me over with excellent features like transcripts and automatic chapters.

My main hesitation in recommending the Podcasts app, however, has been its confusing Up Next queue. Thankfully, iOS 27.2 delivers a long-awaited fix.

In iOS 27.2, the Home tab in Apple Podcasts splits Up Next into two separate sections: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

These new sections offer, in my view, a much better system than what was there before. I no longer lose track of episodes I’ve previously started, since they’re not getting replaced by new episodes in my queue. Instead, there’s a clear divide between what’s new and what’s in-progress.

Shared Albums have long been one of my favorite features in Apple Photos. I don’t post on social media often, but I do love sharing photos and videos with close family and friends via the Photos app.

iOS 27 brought big upgrades to Shared Albums, the first notable changes in years. And to my surprise, Apple has already introduced even more improvements with iOS 27.2. Per Apple:

Shared Albums in Photos adds the ability to edit captions and comments, to avoid adding duplicate photos, and can display a reminder before albums expire so participants can save important photos and videos

Support for editing captions and comments is long overdue, but a welcome addition. I also love the prompt that helps prevent duplicate photos, because I always find myself needing to double-check if I’ve shared certain photos already—now I don’t have to anymore.

There are a ton of other great additions in iOS 27.2, which you can read about below:

Naturally, given the time of year, there are plenty of holiday movies now streaming on Paramount+, but making my pick was easy as Paramount+ just added my personal favorite Christmas film of all time. If you're not quite ready for festive-themed streaming, however, I'm also highlighting an iconic Sylvester Stallone action-thriller and an overlooked WWII drama.

Don't waste your weekend scrolling through the more than 120 movies just added to Paramount+. Here are the three that need to be at the very top of your watchlist.

"It's a Wonderful Life" is practically mandatory viewing over the holiday season. This 1946 Frank Capra classic isn't just the best Christmas movie of all time, but one of the greatest films of the 20th century. Charming, warm and sentimental, it celebrates the true reason for the season in quite some style. It's a feel-good movie that almost every new holiday movie takes inspiration from; it's quite simply a timeless masterpiece.

James Stewart stars as George Bailey, a selfless man who has given up his own dreams to help his family and community. On Christmas Eve, he reaches rock bottom and considers suicide. However, his guardian angel, Clarence (Henry Travers), intervenes and shows George what a lesser place the world would be if he had never existed. Also starring Donna Reed and Lionel Barrymore, "It's a Wonderful Life" lives up to its sterling reputation.

Watch "It's a Wonderful Life" on Paramount+ now

Sylvester Stallone's John Rambo is one of the 1980s most iconic action heroes, which makes his debut, "First Blood," a little peculiar. Sequels would depict Rambo as an unstoppable killing machine, but in his first outing, he's a traumatized soldier, scarred by what he saw and what he did during the Vietnam War. In fact, Rambo kills only a single person in the entire movie, and even that death is typically classified as accidental.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

If you're looking for '80s action pulp, go for one of the sequels, but if you want a tense thriller, then stream "First Blood." In my books, it's the best Rambo film of the lot. In "First Blood," Rambo (Stallone) finds himself on the wrong side of an arrogant small-town sheriff (Brian Dennehy); their confrontation spirals into a manhunt, as the law attempts to capture Rambo. But this former Special Forces soldier is a tricky man to catch.

The above picks are legendary movies. While they're still exceptional in 2026, you may have seen them before. So, for my final option this week, I'm going for "Allied." Directed by Robert Zemeckis (the filmmaker behind "Cast Away" and "Contact"), this 2016 wartime romantic drama stars Brad Pitt and Marion Cotillard. It was a box office flop and received lukewarm reviews upon release, but I believe it's worthy of a second chance.

Opening in 1942, during World War II, operative Max Vatan (Pitt) is paired with a French Resistance fighter, Marianne Beauséjour (Cotillard). The two pose as a married couple as part of a plan to assassinate a German ambassador, only for their pretend romance to become real. They settle in London, get married, have a baby, and all seems well. That is, until Max is informed by his superiors that Marianne might just be a German spy.

When he’s not reviewing the latest games, searching for hidden gems on Netflix, or writing hot takes on new gaming hardware, TV shows and movies, he can be found attending music festivals and getting far too emotionally invested in his favorite football team.

#3517. Focker In Law First Reactions Are Officially In

Focker-In-Law is already the talk of the town.

The Meet the Parents franchise is a multi-film comedy movie series centered on the cultural and lifestyle clashes between the uptight Byrnes family and the free-spirited Focker family. The franchise began in 2000 with the release of Meet the Parents, starring Robert De Niro and Ben Stiller, based on an independent movie released in 1992. Since then, two sequels have followed: 2004's Meet the Fockers and 2010's Little Fockers. After 16 years, Stiller and De Niro are returning to the beloved comedy.

Movie lovers and critics alike can watch the newest installment of the Meet the Parents franchise, Focker-In-Law, before its release on November 25. The new movie follows Greg Focker's (played by Stiller) son Henry (played by Skyler Gisondo) as he brings his trained FBI hostage negotiator girlfriend, Olivia (played by Ariana Grande), home to meet the family, leading to chaos and mayhem. First reactions to the iconic comedy franchise's return are officially in.

ScreenRant's Tatiana Hullender shared her thoughts on Focker-In-Law, praising Grande for meeting Stiller's stellar comedic timing in the best way by stating, "Focker-In-Law was such a fun and fresh movie! Seeing Ariana Grande go toe-to-toe with Ben Stiller was a blast, as Skyler Gisondo is adorkably lovable. Certified good time at the cinema!"

The Genre of Your Life podcast host, Doug Jones, shared a similar sentiment regarding Focker-In-Law, and even went as far to say that Grande "steals the show." "#FockerInLaw is a Focking good time! Perfect for the whole family & just in time for the holidays! Charmingly cute, hilarious & has a ton of heart. It captures everything that made the original so beloved & special. The new cast members are stellar & Ariana Grande steals the show," shared Jones.

The Grande praise keeps on coming, as writer and critic Bill Bria stated, "For the Ariana fans in my mentions: yes, she’s excellent in it. Proves that she gets the tone of the material. And, while she can be broad when it’s required, she’s mostly subtle and grounded, which sells the comedy even better." Bria continued and shared, "FOCKER-IN-LAW is the most unexpectedly pleasant surprise. Rather than lazily flipping the script of MEET THE PARENTS (or repeating it), John Hamburg & co. make a clever direct sequel that’s reliant on the top notch cast, with Ben Stiller being MVP. Some belly laughs in this one!"

Critic Christopher Rates It went so far as to state that Grande's presence would've been missed thanks to her charm and comedic timing. He stated:

"In all honesty, Focker-in-Law is funnier and better than you’d initially expect.

The combined chemistry of Ben Stiller, Robert De Niro, Ariana Grande, and Skyler Gisondo makes this just a simple fine watch to wind down. It feels reminiscent of the original and has some hilarious set pieces here and there but is ultimately bogged down by falling into legacy sequel tropes and some moments that feel out of place.

It’s a film that truthfully wouldn’t be the same without Ariana Grande’s charm, comedic timing, and ability to shift tones without it feeling jarring."

Editor and film critic Edward Douglas guarantees that laughter will arise when enjoying watching Focker-In-Law upon its global theatrical release on November 25. Douglas shared a post on X with a small review of the comedy movie and stated, "I just got back from an early screening of Focker-in-Law, and I was not expecting to laugh as much as I did, mainly because I'd seen the trailer so many times and was nervous those were the biggest laughs... nope... and the movie gives a lot more context to those jokes as well."

Another early review came from Brandon Davis gave for Focker-In-Law, which really makes clear that this is a perfect family movie by stating, "#FockerInLaw is a really fun time. It’s a bit over-the-top like a classic comedy at times and still reels it in for surprisingly touching end. Ariana is really good, Ben Stiller & Robert De Niro are committed & comedic as ever. My Mom is gonna love it."

That Hollywood Show's Editor-in-Chief, Junior Felix, goes as far as to claim Focker-In-Law is "the funniest films of the year." Felix shared his early thoughts on X and stated, "#FockerInLaw is one of the funniest films of the year! I had an absolute blast watching this film and genuinely was not ready for the amount of times I would die laughing. Ariana Grande is a damn treasure and has some hilarious moments. This is the pitch perfect family comedy we really need right now and it's the gift that keeps giving. Also, Eduardo Franco is HYSTERICAL!"

Focker-In-Law heads to theaters on November 25.

#3516. Forget 'Fallout,' Netflix’s New Sci-Fi Western Officially Rides Onto Streaming

The Wild West has been the hope of some of the most notorious outlaws out there over the years but sometimes, outlaws or ordinary old gunslingers aren't quite enough for the story some people want to tell. And that's exactly the case with Netflix's latest series that mixes the sci-fi wasteland elements of Fallout and the adult adnimation of Arcane.

Netflix's new animated Sci-Fi Western Bass X Machina officially premieres on November 3, 2026, bringing an unusual blend of steampunk technology, supernatural horror, and Western action to the streaming service. Created by LeSean Thomas (Yasuke), the six-episode series features animation from Studio Mir, the acclaimed studio behind The Legend of Korra and The Witcher: Nightmare of the Wolf.

In a lawless Steampunk West overrun by brutal outlaws, machines, and supernatural terrors, a father is forced to become judge, jury, and executioner — knowing that every act of justice meant to protect his family may ultimately cost him the very people he’s fighting to save.

The voice cast is led by Brian Tyree Henry (Atlanta) as Bass, alongside Janelle Monáe (Glass Onion: A Knives Out Mystery) as Glory, Tati Gabrielle (The Last of Us) as Dana, Cree Summer (Rugrats) as Ahni, Chaske Spencer (The Twilight Saga: New Moon) as Lighthorse, Currie Graham (Reacher) as Rivenbark, and Starletta DuPois (The Notebook) as Etta.

The series is executive produced by Henry, Thomas, Jennifer Wiley-Moxley, and Chad Handley, with original music composed by Roman GianArthur Irvin and Nate Wonder through Wondaland. Netflix originally planned to release the show in October before shifting its debut to November.

Bass X Machina has also launched with a stunning 100% score on Rotten Tomatoes, which is a signal that the series is one to be taken seriously. In fact, by comparison, it is officially one of the best-reviewed Western television series of all time, as well as one of the highest-rated science fiction shows ever produced, not just by Netflix, but by any streaming platform. That puts it alongside some of the streamer’s most acclaimed animated originals, including Arcane.

All six episodes of Bass X Machina arrived on Netflix on November 3, 2026. Stay tuned to Collider for all the latest news and updates on what's currently streaming on Netflix.

November 2026 is here, which means a bunch of new titles are coming to top streaming services like Prime Video. And this weekend has a delightful mix of options where new TV shows are concerned, whether you're into boxing dramas, college romances or buddy thrillers.

First up is "The Greatest," an eight-part limited series centered on legendary American boxer and activist Muhammad Ali; the Prime Video bio-drama marks the first time that Ali's estate has fully approved and signed off on a scripted series about the boxing icon's life.

If you like your fighting to look more like an enemies-to-lovers dynamic, check out "Campus Drivers," a new college-set romance series based on a super-popular BookTok favorite. And if you want your crime drama with a side of lighthearted banter and buddy chemistry, tune into "Chaar Yaar," a new Hindi-language thriller set in early-aughts Mumbai.
