What is it about: You know him as Muhammad Ali, arguably the greatest heavyweight boxer of all time, but this eight-episode bio-drama lets you in on the young fella named Cassius Clay. In this first-ever authorized scripted series on the iconic prizefighter, we catch up with Clay (Jaalen Best) fresh off his landmark gold medal win at the 1960 Olympics, following the athlete as he sets his sights on the Heavyweight Championship and contends with newfound fame, family conflicts, and political strife along the way.

#3512. Why I'd Choose the Oura Ring 5 Over the Cheaper Ultrahuman Pro

Ultrahuman’s Ring Pro is now officially on sale in the U.S., which makes this the perfect time to consider how this new device compares to the reigning champ in the smart ring market, the Oura Ring 5. Here's the short answer: While there’s a lot to like in the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, ultimately I think the Oura Ring 5 is just better at doing its job.

I’ve spent plenty of time with both rings, and admittedly, many of the differences between the two will come down to personal preference—for example, do you like the biohacking concept and the “next best actions” suggestions in the Ultrahuman app, or do you favor the soothing vibes of the Oura app? But when it comes to the devices themselves, there are big differences between them in terms of size, cost, and overall ease of use. Here’s my take on each, and why Oura is still my top choice.

The Oura Ring 5 is impressively small, and when you have to wear something on your finger, size matters a lot—and generally, smaller is better. The Oura Ring 5 is the smallest and most comfortable smart ring I’ve ever worn. I have a ton of photos here comparing it in size to other smart rings (including RingConn, older Oura rings, and an older Ultrahuman); suffice it to say, the Oura Ring 5 wins this category easily.

When it comes to the interior fit, both rings are similar: mostly smooth on the inside, without any intrusive bumps. But considering the overall shape and feel, the Oura Ring 5 is just more comfortable to wear throughout an entire day.

The Oura Ring 5 comes with a plug-in charger, which isn’t very convenient, but will get the job done. You can buy a slim, rounded charging case that easily fits in your pocket for $99. You need to match the size of the case to the size of your ring, and the charging case is not compatible with earlier versions of the device. It’s good for 30 days of charge, according to Oura.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro comes with a charging case that is heavy and bulky with prominent corners, but good for an extra 45 days of battery life. The case fits any size of Ultrahuman Ring Pro, but is not compatible with previous versions. You can have the case play sounds if you’ve misplaced it.

The Ultrahuman ring lasts slightly longer on a charge: eight to 10 days, according to the company, versus six to nine for the Oura Ring 5. The Ultrahuman ring also has several different battery modes, with “chill mode” lasting me about two weeks.

To sum up: the Ultrahuman ring lasts longer on a charge and has more capacity in its charging case. You also get the charging case for free. But the Oura Ring 5’s charging case is smaller and much easier to carry around. Once again, we’re looking at two decent options: The Oura case is more expensive for what you get, but it’s also nicer to use.

Oura is the most expensive smart ring out there, and it requires a subscription. That makes it the priciest option, giving Ultrahuman an opening to beat it simply by virtue of being cheaper. But this one is closer to a wash, depending on the choices you make. If you’re looking for the cheapest possible smart ring, well, you’d probably end up with something else entirely, like a RingConn Air. But between the Oura Ring 5 and the Ultrahuman Ring Pro, the latter is cheaper than the Oura Ring 5...but only if you’re saying no to all the extras. Let me break it down.

The Oura Ring 5 costs $399 for the shiny black and silver models, and $499 for gold, rose, and the matte versions of the black and silver. The subscription costs $5.99/month (or $69.99/year, which is only a $2 savings), and the Oura is basically useless without the subscription.

Here's how the cost works out on an annual basis:

Oura Ring 5 in black or silver: $399 + $5.99/month subscription = $470.88 for one year, $542.76 for two years

Oura Ring 5 in other colors: $499 + $5.99/month subscription = $570.88 for one year, $642.76 for two years.

The Ultrahuman Ring Pro is $479 for all colors, and there is no subscription for basic use of the ring. But you can't necessarily stop there, because the Ultrahuman app includes “PowerPlugs” that will give you extra features or analysis screens. Some are totally free, including the caffeine window,  smart alarms, a new parent mode, and a limited version of the cycle and ovulation tracker, but others carry a monthly fee. And if you consider all the optional subscription fees for different PowerPlugs, they can quickly add up:

HealthEx, to connect medical records: $4.99/month

Most people probably wouldn't choose all of them, but even if you just wanted, say, respiratory health and cycle & ovulation pro, you’d quickly outstrip the price of an Oura Ring’s subscription. On the other hand, Ultrahuman also offers an Ultrahuman Max plan for $9.99/month or $99.99/year that includes all the PowerPlugs mentioned above, plus the Les Mills workouts that normally run $11.99/month. That's cheaper than subscribing to all of the options individually, but it will also make the Ultrahuman Ring Pro more expensive than the Oura Ring 5: $578.99 total for one year, or $678.98 for two years. In short, if you want everything that each ring has to offer, the Ultrahuman will cost you more.

Here's the big caveat: I wouldn't recommend bothering with most of the PowerPlugs. For example, "UltraSync for Tesla" recommends settings for your car based on how rested you are, which will be useless if you don't have a Tesla, and probably even if you do. "Cardio adaptability" measures a metric that Ultrahuman says is subtly different from HRV; Oura doesn't measure this adaptability metric, but it's not clear to me whether it's even worth measuring at all (I'd argue probably not).

Ultrahuman's respiratory health PowerPlug ($3.99/month) records sounds while you sleep, which Oura doesn't do; but Oura reports breathing disturbances based on the ring's data, which Ultrahuman doesn't do. Ultrahuman's feature is more expensive.

Ultrahuman offers a premium version of its cycle tracker for $3.99/month, while Oura has a partnership with Natural Cycles that cost $149.99/year. Either will provide more detailed (and, each company says, more accurate) cycle tracking than the basic tracking each app provides without the extras. Oura's option is more expensive.

Ultrahuman's HealthEx Powerplug ($4.99/month) displays information from your medical records throughout the app; Oura lets you import your medical records for free, but uses them mainly in the Advisor (chatbot) and dedicated areas of the app. Ultrahuman's option is more expensive.

Oura's app gives you scores for your readiness, sleep, and recent activity, and it tracks how stressed you seem to be throughout the day. A message at the top of the main screen gives you advice for what to do that day—for example, scaling back your workouts if you seem to be tired or stressed. Ultrahuman does pretty much the same thing, giving you a "next best action" that changes throughout the day, but tends to stick to predictable themes: get more activity if you've been sitting, and that sort of thing.

Both give detailed breakdowns of the factors that contribute to your scores, and both likely overstate how useful their scores are (you don't actually need to change your workout plans just because you had a less-than-perfect night of sleep). But the apps handle the basics pretty similarly: Both have partners and integrations, and you can book blood tests through either app, if you want to do that for some reason.

Ultrahuman gives you a bit more guidance on circadian rhythms, urging you to get in extra steps during certain times of day, and offering to micromanage your caffeine intake. It has a "longevity" tab that puts your long-term habits in terms of how many years they are supposedly subtracting from (or adding to) your lifespan, including measurable metrics like VO2max and a few things that are more inscrutable, like arterial stiffness.

Oura has a whole tab of "vitals" that it calculates from your day-to-day data, which I find more useful than Ultrahuman's data views. The items here include "resilience," which compares your stress to your recovery; a "symptom radar" that can sometimes flag when you're sick; and metrics of sleep regularity and how you're breathing. And, of course, you can check your "cardiovascular age" to see how much younger (or older) you should feel.

Overall, I prefer Oura's approach because the metrics make more sense, are easier to find, and are less likely to feel like they're going way out on a limb relative to the underlying science. Ultrahuman wants you to feel like a cutting-edge biohacker; Oura does a bit more to keep things down to earth. It is a bit funny to remember that both apps, and their wealth of data, are basically just pulling from heart rate readings throughout the day and night. Neither app gives you any truly important information the other doesn't, but Oura's makes more sense to me.

#3511. NBC Sets Up The End Of Network TV’s Longest Era

Cher Thompson is a Senior Staff Writer at Screen Rant, where she covers everything from explosive reality TV moments to cast interviews about the twists and turns of scripted dramas. With a background in creative writing, marketing, and teaching, Cher knows how to spot both the storytelling genius and the guilty pleasures in pop culture. Her work blends wit with insight, making readers feel like they’re chatting with a friend who just happens to know way too much about TV.

With its milestone 600th episode coming soon, Law & Order: Special Victims Unit is setting itself up for milestone after milestone, as well as the end of network TV's longest era yet. Having been on the air since 1999, Law & Order: SVU has become a cornerstone of NBC's slate of procedurals, stretching across decades and bringing even the most intense cases to life. From stories that are ripped from the headlines to intense character-driven cases, the series has become one of the most well-known and in-depth procedurals throughout its time on the air, building its own characters into the narrative.

With Mariska Hargitay's Olivia Benson becoming a fixture on the series quickly, the current Captain wasn't alone in the fight against New York's most heinous crimes. Throughout the earliest seasons of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, Benson was partnered with detective Elliot Stabler (Christopher Meloni), who spent years on the series working alongside her. While Stabler left SVU in 2011, Meloni has returned to the series several times over the past 15 years, even anchoring his own series in the past few seasons, the now defunct Law & Order: Organized Crime. As one of SVU's defining characters, Stabler's one of Benson's closest connections.

With Organized Crime having come to an end on the heels of Special Victims Unit reaching a major milestone, Stabler's return to the series felt like kismet. It's also possible that his next reunion with Benson, during Law & Order: Special Victims Unit's 600th episode, could mark the end of one of NBC's longest and most agonizing eras.

While Stabler has returned to Law & Order: SVU in the past, seeing him in the upcoming 600th episode will be different for viewers, especially with this being his first appearance in the franchise post-Organized Crime. Stabler will be joining Benson in an investigation during Law & Order: Special Victims Unit season 28 episode 6, "Obedience," which will see the pair being tasked with revisiting one of their first cases together. As new leads come to light, Benson and Stabler will have to confront the mistakes and subsequent consequences of the choices they made in the past, which may change their present, too.

The premise of Law & Order: SVU's 600th episode calls into question the expertise of Benson and Stabler, and at the same time tasks them with an interesting new lens to look at their relationship from. While the professional aspect of having to retrace their steps from over 25 years prior is fascinating, bringing Stabler back into the mix to revisit a case is hardly the only thing that viewers will be anticipating from the episode. After years of slow-burning potential from Benson and Stabler, the chance to look at their past from a new perspective could give the pair a significant push forward.

While the episode doesn't necessarily have to turn romantic for Benson and Stabler, revisiting their past in a meticulous way could make for an interesting avenue for the characters to explore how things have changed. With their relationship consistently shifting and bending, the connection between the pair could find a new path during SVU's milestone hour.

For over a decade of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, Benson and Stabler's partnership was close and personal, but never romantically charged despite some viewers hoping it would turn. Though Benson was typically single, Law & Order: SVU quickly established that Stabler was married with a family, and the series chose not to shift that dynamic to incorporate Benson into the mix. While Stabler's relationship wasn't always stable, it was clear that his partnership with Benson was a close connection that SVU wasn't going to complicate by putting romantic feelings on the table. Later, however, the series began to push a different agenda.

When Stabler's wife, Kathy, died prior to the launch of Law & Order: Organized Crime, a completely different path forward opened up for the Benson and Stabler connection. Now, long harbored respect and slow simmering romance was bubbling up to the surface, and it became clear that though there were never moments where the pair were going to act on those feelings prior, Benson and Stabler's chemistry was vastly different. Their relationship continued to grow more complicated as Benson and Stabler went through their own moments of hardship, but found one another there as support despite their professional tether all but snapping.

With Law & Order: SVU consistently bringing Benson and Stabler close to the brink of something more, even seeing the pair nearly kiss in a recent season, the former partners have never actually crossed that line. The 600th episode could be the perfect time for the former partners to try something new, especially with the show opening up their past to a completely different interpretation.

Though anything is possible in the world of Law & Order: Special Victims Unit, it doesn't necessarily feel like the show will ever truly feature Benson and Stabler in a supportive, happy romance, at least not in the way viewers might expect. While there's a compelling reason to push through and see Benson and Stabler finally pursue a relationship, the idea of putting the characters together only to have the bulk of their romance be off-screen doesn't offer the level of pay off that viewers would want. The tension between the characters, however, is still something that can keep the hope of a romance alive and well.

While there may not be a happy ending on the horizon for Benson and Stabler any time soon, the idea that something may shift between the characters in the Law & Order: SVU 600th episode isn't impossible. With a near-kiss already having happened on screen, there's a clear desire between the characters, and that points to something further taking place in the future, whether that's a near future or a far one. Hargitay has always spoken highly of Meloni and their work together, and bringing Stabler back into the mix almost always promises some great moments for the pair.

With a happy ending far from guaranteed, Law & Order: Special Victims Unit has always been in the habit of surprising its viewers, which could mean the Benson and Stabler story may well find itself changing for the better. Though it's not necessarily likely, it's definitely possible that Law & Order: Special Victims Unit's milestone episode could end the will they/won't they era for Benson and Stabler.

Following last week’s release of macOS 27.2, Apple has now kicked off the next round of beta testing with the first developer beta of macOS 27.3 Golden Gate. Here are the details.

It’s been an unusually eventful few weeks for Mac users. In addition to several security releases for macOS Tahoe 26.7.2 and macOS Sequoia 15.8.2, Apple released macOS 27.2 Golden Gate lats week, with expanded language support for Siri AI and new conversation recall capabilities.

On the hardware side, Apple recently announced new M6-powered iMacs and 14-inch MacBook Pro, and the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display “with Touch,” as Apple has been addressing it.

macOS 27.3 also brings several new features to Safari, including Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and the ability to organize tabs using Siri AI. You can read more about those changes here.

The update also comes as Apple prepares to launch Apple Intelligence in China with iOS 27.3. However, the company has confirmed that the initial rollout will be exclusive to the iPhone, with support for other platforms coming only after the necessary regulatory approvals have been obtained.

macOS 27.3 may also most likely include further under-the-hood refinements to the macOS interface to accommodate touchscreen input, building on the new gesture recognition tools introduced in macOS 27.2.

#3509. 10 Perfect Miniseries Based on Books, Ranked

It was in the UK back during the '50s and '60s that the miniseries format was born, still named "television serials" before the term "miniseries" was coined in the US in the '70s. Indeed, it was American networks who adopted, rebranded, and greatly popularized the format precisely around that time. Since then, the small screen has offered hundreds upon hundreds of masterful miniseries worthy of being counted among the greatest shows of all time.

Though many of those exceptional miniseries have been fully original stories, many others have been adapted from previously-existing material, including several books. It could be a miniseries based on a great, foundational classic of literature, such as 1995's Pride and Prejudice; or one based on a non-fiction book about much more modern events, like Dopesick. Regardless, these are some of the best miniseries of all time.

Before the American remake became the first-ever Netflix original series, the BBC adapted Michael Dobbs' House of Cards, the first political thriller novel in the trilogy of the same title. This is the story of Conservative Party chief whip Francis Urquhart, a Machiavellian politician who rises to power right after the end of Margaret Thatcher's tenure as Prime Minister of the UK.

It's also one of those rare screen adaptations whose quality surpasses that of the source material.

It's far and away one of the greatest British miniseries of the '90s, with a career-defining performance by Rian Richardson and some absolutely perfect use of fourth-wall-breaking. What's more, it's also one of those rare screen adaptations whose quality surpasses that of the source material. The show perfectly captures the Shakespearean qualities of Dobbs' book, while adding plenty of its own unique spice.

Elizabeth Gaskell's 1854 novel North and South is a true cornerstone of Victorian literature, and it has been adapted for the small screen thrice. There's a strong argument to be made in favor of the fourt-part version starring Richard Armitage and Daniela Denby-Ashe being the best of the bunch, as it perfectly recounts the story of a privileged young woman relocating herself to an industrial mill town, where her initial clash with a stern cotton mill owner slowly transforms into a deep romance.

The sizzling chemistry between Armitage and Denby-Ashe practically oozes through the screen in every scene they share; which, combined with the show's top-tier production values and nuanced writing, makes for an absolutely faultless adaptation of one of the most acclaimed English-language Victorian novels. Both those who love the source material and those who have never read it should love this incredible miniseries.

She was already a well-known name in Hollywood by the time Netflix's The Queen's Gambit came out, but it was this exceptional miniseries that really launched Anya Taylor-Joy into serious, award-worthy superstardom. This is based on Walter Tevis' 1983 novel, following an orphaned chess prodigy battling addiction and personal demons as she rises through the male-dominated ranks to become an international grandmaster.

It's one of the best Netflix shows with less than 40 episodes, bolstered by the incredible writing just as much as it is by Taylor-Joy's unforgettable turn as Beth Harmon. It's a mesmerizingly complex antihero story that makes every chess movement feel like an element from an adrenaline-pumping thriller, greatly elevating the entertainment value of the source material while staying quite faithful to its narrative skeleton.

Four Netflix characters, four completely different ways of showing up for somebody. This is the one who fits how you actually do friendship, and what having them in your life would be like.

You do not do friendship at half volume, and neither does he. What you want is somebody who says yes to the plan before you have finished describing the plan.

You are the friend who makes things happen, and so is she. Together you would be mildly exhausting to everyone around you and completely delighted with yourselves.

You have no patience for pleasant lies, and she has no ability to tell them. What looks like coldness from the outside is the most reliable friendship on this list.

You look after whoever is having the worst day. So does he. It is the least strategic way to move through the world and the best possible quality in a friend.

By this point, Mike Flanagan has already firmly established himself as one of the modern kings of horror television, but even the greats have to start somewhere. In his case, that was his first-ever show: The Haunting of Hill House, based on Shirley Jackson's 1859 novel, about a family forced to reunite years after their mother's mysterious death after another tragedy draws them back to the mansion that still holds them captive.

Many would go so far as to say that it's one of the best miniseries ever made, which makes it unsurprising that it turned Flanagan into such a household name. There are hugely effective elements of horror, but what really fuels the story is the emotional and thematic depth of its narrative. It may not be all that faithful to Jackson's classic in terms of plot, but it captures the book's spirit marvelously.

Kevin Sullivan's CBC classic Anne of Green Gables can be viewed as either a two-part miniseries or a made-for-television film. Regardless, one thing remains certain: This is a cornerstone of televisual Canadian pop culture. Based on the eponymous book by Canadian icon Lucy Maud Montgomery, the miniseries follows a spirited orphaned girl who's taken in by an aging brother and sister on Prince Edward Island, her fierce charm slowly transforming their lives and the local community.

Though its DNA is as passionately and warmly Canadian as that of Montgomery's book, this is as universally endearing of a small-screen story as they come, full of exceptional performances and breathtaking PEI and rural Ontario vistas. It's the sort of miniseries so irresistibly charming and emotionally complex that it's virtually impossible to watch it and not enjoy it at least a little bit.

The subject of both the Hulu masterpiece Dopesick and the non-fiction book it's based on, Dopesick: Dealers, Doctors, and the Drug Company that Addicted America is the story of the company that triggered the worst drug epidemic in American history. What follows that premise is one of the best crime miniseries of all time, one as insightful as it is deeply human and admirably dramatic.

How can one even begin singing the praises of such a perfect show? For one, there's the star-studded cast, featuring top-tier performances by actors like Michael Keaton and Kaitlyn Dever. Then, there's the multi-perspective framing, which lends the story an air of raw realism. All in all, it's an incredible adaptation that fuses the journalistic spirit of its source material with deeply sensitive and faithful narrative drama.

The question of what single book is most worthy of the elusive title of "The Great American Novel" is a debate that's probably destined to never have one satisfying answer, but there's a certain title that's thrown around far more often than most: Larry McMurtry's Lonesome Dove. This just so happens to be the source material of the greatest Western TV miniseries the world has ever seen.

One of the best 8-episodes-or-less masterpiece miniseries in history, Lonesome Dove is both deeply faithful to the legendary book and uniquely strong when analyzed in a vacuum. It's a masterful de-mythologization of the American Frontier and the tropes it carries with it, anchored by Basil Poledouris' incredible music and the jaw-droppingly perfect work of stars like Robert Duvall and Tommy Lee Jones.

Jane Austen's Pride and Prejudice, about the eventful relationship between the quick-witted Elizabeth and the wealthy Mr. Darcy, is such a crucial pillar of English literature that adapting it is always a titanic task. In the eyes of many fans, no one has ever been more successful than Andrew Davies, whose BBC adaptation is far and away the most perfect version of the story that the screen has ever been graced with.

One of the miniseries with the most perfect pacing and most wonderful writing, Pride and Prejudice mainly benefits from Colin Firth and Jennifer Ehle displaying some of the most unbelievable chemistry that any actor-actress duo has ever displayed in a miniseries. Full of iconic moments, luxurious visuals, and loving fidelity to Austen's classic, it's a must-see for anyone who doesn't have a heart of stone.

Based on the historical novels I, Claudius and Claudius the God by Robert Graves, the BBC's I, Claudius is one of those near-perfect miniseries that have been tragically forgotten as the years have passed. Nonetheless, this retelling of the history of the early Roman Empire from the perspective of Emperor Claudius still remains one of the highest-rated miniseries in history on IMDb.

That praise is all for good reason. It's an absolutely brilliant adaptation that marvelously condenses two super-complex novels into a seamless 12-episode narrative, darkly satirical and absolutely Shakespearean in tone. On top of being visually and narratively impressive, it's also a masterclass in classical acting, including the top-notch performances of actors like Derek Jacobi, John Hurt, and Patrick Stewart.

For years, HBO's Band of Brothers, executive-produced by Tom Hanks and Steven Spielberg, has been the highest-rated miniseries of all time on IMDb. It's such a masterful show that that's likely to never change. Based on the 1992 non-fiction book of the same title by historian Stephen E. Ambrose, it's one of the best-ever HBO miniseries based on books, and then some.

There's the incredible performances of the stacked cast, including actors of the stature of Damian Lewis, David Schwimmer, Michael Fassbender, and Tom Hardy. There's the way the show, much like Hanks and Spielberg's Saving Private Ryan, captures the brutality of World War II combat with unmatched realism and humanism. There's the deep emotional resonance of the way the book explores themes of brotherhood and leadership. From top to bottom and from beginning to end, Band of Brothers is not only an immensely faithful adaptation of an excellent non-fiction book, but genuinely one of the greatest works in television history.

#3508. Five Creative Ways to Spend Your FSA Funds Before the End of the Year

If you have a flexible spending account (FSA), you know the drill: Use the funds before the end of the year, or lose them. Unfortunately, chances are slim you can pack the rest of the year with doctor's appointments. Does that mean your hard-earned funds go to waste? Definitely not. You can spend your remaining FSA funds on other qualifying healthcare costs. And what counts as "qualifying" might surprise you—for instance, you can use your FSA or HSA funds to get yourself a sweet new fitness tracker or smartwatch.

As the end of the year approaches, here are all the ways you can spend any leftover money in your FSA balance.

Many over-the-counter medications and health items are FSA-eligible, including pain relievers, cold medicine, bandages, dental care products, menstrual products, and more. Scan your medicine cabinet and make a list of anything you need to stock up on.

FSA/HSA eligibility for smartwatches and other fitness wearables is real, but the main “catch" (as I’ve previously explained) is proving the device is in fact necessary, which requires you to obtain a Letter of Medical Necessity (LMN).

Screenless recovery trackers like Whoop, Amazfit Helio Strap, and the Oura Ring can usually be justified as HSA/FSA eligible around sleep quality, HRV-based stress monitoring, or recovery tracking tied to a chronic condition. Similarly, smartwatches can qualify the same way a basic tracker does, as long as you can link a relevant documented health concern. For instance, Coros offers FSA/HSA eligibility for all its watches and heart rate monitors through its partnership with Truemed. Amazfit similarly lets you filter by HSA/FSA eligibility for its smartwatches.

If you want to get creative with it, the official FSA store lets you filter by "surprisingly eligible." Similar to the section above, for some of these items, you'll want to brush up on how exactly to get an LMN to justify certain tech as FSA-eligible for you personally. In the meantime, go crazy and snag yourself Epsom salt for $8.99, Supergoop! sunscreen for $38.00, or perhaps a snazzy massage gun for $349.99.

Knee braces, wrist splints, compression socks, and other orthopedic items can help relieve chronic pain issues. Rather than wait for these issues to rear their heads down the line, use FSA money to offset the costs of these fixes now. If you use eyeglasses or contacts, consider using your FSA dollars to update or refresh your prescriptions. Don't forget to stock up on eye drops and lens solution, too.

If you have medical procedures scheduled for early next year, many healthcare providers will allow you to pre-pay the estimated costs this calendar year using FSA funds. This includes dental work, physical therapy, chiropractic visits, Lasik eye surgery, and more.

However you choose to spend your FSA funds, don’t let that money go to waste. After all, it came out of your paycheck. Check in with your employer’s rules for any balance remaining on Dec. 31 this year, so you aren’t left forfeiting your hard-earned funds. You can find a complete list at the FSA store here.

#3505. Apple announces Fitness+ Gym Strength program with personalized workout plans

Apple wants to help you get stronger. Apple Fitness+ is expanding to the gym with a new strength training experience. Gym Strength is now available in beta, bringing personalized workout plans, exercise demonstrations, and Apple Watch logging to your lifting routine.

Gym Strength creates progressive, four-week plans based on your strength goals, experience, schedule, and available equipment. After you complete each week of workouts, the following week adapts based on the reps and weight you logged.

The feature is designed for a range of experience levels, from people trying strength training for the first time to experienced lifters looking to make progress. It also aims to help anyone who wants to build a more consistent routine.

When building a plan, you choose your workout days and the body areas you want to focus on. You can select five exercises per workout, which Apple estimates will take about 20–30 minutes, or seven exercises for about 45–60 minutes, depending on your pace.

Each workout recommends exercises, reps, sets, and how much weight to lift.

You move through the workout at your own pace, with short video demonstrations from Apple Fitness+ trainers available for each exercise. The demonstrations can be expanded to show the movement from three different angles.

Apple says Gym Strength includes over 350 exercises across more than 30 types of strength training equipment, including dumbbells, kettlebells, suspension trainers, cable machines, and barbells. Dumbbells are the minimum equipment requirement.

Plans account for the equipment available to you, so the experience can work in a commercial gym or a home gym.

If a machine is occupied or you’re training somewhere with different equipment, you can swap equipment or choose an alternative exercise with a similar movement and body focus. You can also add sets or skip exercises.

Gym Strength requires an iPhone running iOS 27.3 or an iPad running iPadOS 27.3. An Apple Watch running watchOS 27.3 optionally lets you view exercises and log reps and weight from your wrist, while tracking heart rate and calories burned.

Gym Strength also introduces Training Note, an optional feature powered by Apple Intelligence that previews workouts, explains progression, and highlights milestones. Training Note requires an Apple Intelligence–enabled iPhone or iPad with the device set to English.

Gym Strength is included in the existing Fitness+ subscription. It joins a library of trainer-led workouts spanning 12 workout types, including Strength, HIIT, Yoga, Pilates, Core, Cycling, Rowing, Dance, Kickboxing, treadmill walking and running, and Mindful Cooldown.

Fitness+ also offers guided meditations, personalized recommendations, and Custom Plans for scheduling workouts, with new sessions added every week.

Fitness+ is also included in Apple One Premier, which costs $39.95 per month in the U.S. and bundles Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, Apple News+, and 2TB of iCloud+ storage.

#3504. Man High On Meth Kills Mom, Believed She Was Possessed

An Oregon man who believed his mother was demonically possessed while he was high on meth has been sentenced to life in prison for her murder ... and prosecutors say he had been thinking about killing her for weeks.

38-year-old Ronald Kirk was convicted of second-degree murder and felony possession of a firearm after shooting and killing his 61-year-old mother, Rosa Leyva, inside the home they shared.

Kirk had been living with his mother in her small Gladstone, Oregon home ... but according to FOX12, their relationship was anything but peaceful.

Prosecutors say Leyva had been fed up with her son's drug and alcohol use, explosive temper, and increasingly bizarre behavior ... and by November 2024, she was ready to kick him out.

According to Clackamas County prosecutors, Kirk had become obsessed with exorcisms and demonic possession while using meth ... even telling a friend he believed his own mother was possessed.

And here's where things get even more disturbing.

A month before the murder, Kirk allegedly left a voicemail for his son claiming his grandmother was possessed ... and admitting he had "almost" put a bullet in her head the day before.

Meanwhile, Leyva was becoming increasingly fearful of her son.

On Nov. 8, she sent Kirk a text making it clear she wanted him gone, writing, "You need to leave. I don't want anyone in my house."

There was just one problem ... Kirk had no job, no money, and was financially dependent on his mother.

Between Nov. 8 and Nov. 11, Leyva contacted Gladstone police asking for help because she was afraid of what her son might do.

In home surveillance footage from Nov. 11, later shown to jurors, Leyva could be heard pleading with her son to get help.

"You're higher than a kite. Get some help. Please," she told him.

Sadly, just two weeks later, her worst fears became reality.

On Nov. 26, 2024, Leyva failed to show up for work, immediately raising concerns among her coworkers and friends, who knew about her son's troubling behavior.

When they couldn't get in contact with her, police were called to conduct a welfare check ... and what officers discovered inside the home was horrifying.

Kirk answered the door and casually told officers his mother was inside and hadn't been conscious for about a day.

When officers entered, they found Leyva dead at the dining room table, sitting in front of her laptop with a full glass of wine nearby. Her body was covered in pillowcases, and she had suffered a single gunshot wound to the head.

Investigators later determined Leyva had been killed around 6:45 PM on Nov. 25 ... meaning Kirk had remained inside the home with his mother's body for nearly 24 hours.

"He sat there with his mother's dead body for a full day," Senior Deputy District Attorney Rusty Amos told jurors.

During Kirk's sentencing, his two sons delivered emotional statements about losing their grandmother ... but they had very different messages for their father.

One son, Andre Leyva, told Kirk he had chosen to forgive him despite everything.

"I forgive you. I love you because that's what God does, and I hope prison and God have mercy on your soul," he said.

His older brother, Antonio Leyva, wasn't ready to offer that same forgiveness.

"I know others have already forgiven you, but I am very far from that. And my Grandma Leyva, I don't just miss her; it's more than that," he told the court.

As for Kirk, he told the court he plans to appeal his conviction.

"I was convicted of second-degree murder," Kirk said before sentencing. "I understand and so I'm ready to be sentenced off and close this case."

Kirk was sentenced to life in prison with the possibility of parole after 25 years ... meaning he'll be in his early 60s before he even has a chance at freedom.

#3503. These 10 New Features Are Coming to iOS 27.3

Apple dropped the first developer beta for iOS 27.3 on Tuesday. While this update isn't as large as iOS 27 proper, it's surprisingly feature-filled for a 0.3 update. This is only a beta, so anything could (and likely will) change before Apple officially launches the update. But, as it stands, iOS 27.3 tests 10 new features—including one feature the company trialed in the previous beta.

Technically, anyone with a compatible iPhone can try out iOS 27.3 right now—assuming you enroll your Apple Account in the developer program. But a word of warning: Betas can be temperamental, and could be risky. As such, I'd recommend avoiding the beta until Apple releases the public beta, which comes after a bit more testing to iron out larger issues. Either way, make sure to make a full backup of your iPhone to a Mac or PC first, as issues with the beta could result in permanent data loss.

With watchOS 27, Apple released "Audio Intelligence," a new set of features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4. Audio Intelligence uses the watches' new S11 chip, along with on-device AI and cloud-based AI, to run new features, like Sound Recognition and Shazam (music recognition).

With iOS 27.3, however, the company is now officially testing the other two Audio Intelligence features it originally announced with watchOS 27. First, there's Live Rewind: By double-clicking the watch crown, you can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds of a conversation. Siri Recap, on the other hand, displays summaries of conversations you had that day, in case you need a refresher on any chats you might have otherwise forgotten about,

The company generated some controversy when it first announced these two Audio Intelligence features, since, on the surface, it sounds like these new Apple Watches are essentially spying on people all day long. According to Apple, however, that isn't really the case. The company says Audio Intelligence is private, and never records or stores any audio. No speakers are ever identified, and text results (both transcripts and summaries) are deleted automatically after a set period of time unless the user saves them to the Siri app. You can read more about how Audio Intelligence works here.

Despite their claims, I'm sure there will still be strong feelings surrounding these Audio Intelligence features. We'll have to see whether Apple can prove Live Rewind and Siri Recap aren't all that creepy throughout the iOS 27.3 beta process.

iOS 27.3 also introduces app actions for Siri AI. Apple is testing new abilities for Siri AI, including organizing files, planning events, or adding photos to albums. You could ask Siri to organize your Downloads folder, or delete files that haven't been opened in more than a year. You could ask Siri to find a coffee shop you went to last week, or to save an article to your Reading List in Safari. You could ask Siri to check your calendar and set up a time for an event based on when you're free. You can even ask the assistant to schedule, edit, or unsend messages.

For example, you could ask Siri AI to help you plan a trip with your friends. You could ask the AI to put together a themed playlist in Apple Music, schedule a message to a group about an upcoming trip, organize the websites you've been visiting in Safari into a tab group, and, after the trip, ask Siri to move your best photos to your favorites album. These new actions work in the following apps: Calendar, Files, Finder, Journal, Mail, Maps, Messages, Music, Notes, Photos, Preview, Reminders, Safari, Shortcuts, and Weather. Developers can also add Siri AI app actions support to their own apps.

Apple started testing its new Health app with the iOS 27.2 beta, but pulled the redesign before the official release. Now, with iOS 27.3, the new app is back. The new Health app has a health dashboard for the first time, as well as new features like Health Age and movement assessments. It seems to be pulling from some popular competitor services, hopefully, for the better. For more on the new Health app, check out Lifehacker health editor Beth Skwarecki's explainer.

Continuing on the Health track, iOS 27.3 also introduces "Gym Strength." This is a new Fitness+ feature that offers a personalized four-week strength-training plan. You can customize these plans to meet your goals, experience level, and schedule, and they adapt as you progress. You'll get recommendations based on your experience with exercises, reps, and sets, including video demos for exercises. You can access Gym Strength on both iPhone and iPad, and Apple Watches are optional—though you can log your progress with the wearable if you have it.

Vertical tabs have been a favorite among browser aficionados, as they give you more screen real estate in your browser while keeping your tabs off the side. Apple hasn't made the jump—until now. This feature works with iPads running iPadOS 27.3 as well as Macs running macOS 27.3.

Another new Safari feature in testing is "Adaptive Dark Mode." This feature forces websites into a dark theme, if they don't have a native theme of their own. There are third-party apps that can do this, but this is the first time Apple has offered this feature built into Safari.

Apple is also testing new StandBy experiences with iOS 27.3, which were previously only available on the iPhone Duo. When you turn your iPhone sideways while plugged in, you'll find new Analog and Digital Clock faces with new customization options. There's also a new Photos face, with the option to pull images from Shared Albums.

"Reachability" pulls your iPhone's display down towards the bottom of the screen, so you can access items towards the top of the display with one hand. It's a useful feature for those of us with big iPhones, and now, there's no iPhone bigger than the Duo. With iOS 27.3, Apple is testing Reachability for its first foldable phone. It's a bit like the inverse of how Reachability currently works: You can swipe on the left or right side of your Duo's display to shift the other side of the screen towards your current position. If you're holding your Duo in your left hand, a swipe of the left side will pull the right side over to the left, and vice versa.

Apple is also rolling out new languages for Siri AI in iOS 27.3. Now, Apple's smart assistant supports Traditional Chinese, Vietnamese, Turkish, and Norwegian.

If you have an Apple Intelligence-compatible iPad running iPadOS 27.3, you now have access to Siri Mode in Camera. As with iOS, you can open the Camera app on iPadOS to access Siri Mode, and ask Siri about your surroundings.

#3502. iOS 27.3 adds all-new Apple Health app, details here

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, and it reintroduces the all-new Health app that was first available for testing during the iOS 27.2 beta. Here’s what’s new.

iOS 27.3 will launch with an upgraded Apple Health app. The new app was initially tested during the iOS 27.2 beta, but it’s back today in iOS 27.3 beta 1 and will ship to all users next month.

Today on Apple Newsroom, the company outlined what to expect from the new Health experience.

Three central new Health features are highlighted for iOS 27.3:

Insights tab: “surfaces timely, holistic summaries spanning heart, sleep, readiness, fitness, vitals, and cycle tracking data throughout the day. A dedicated For You section delivers intelligent recommendations tailored to a user’s daily habits — such as practical guidance to adjust a wind-down routine following consecutive nights of interrupted sleep. The app pairs data with dynamic health content, offering educational videos and articles featuring Health app clinical experts.”

Longevity tab: “analyzes longitudinal metrics across heart health, sleep, mental wellbeing, movement, metabolic health, hearing, and nutrition. Central to this tab is Health Age, a feature that translates data from Apple Watch — including VO2 max, resting heart rate, sleep, and heart rate variability — into a metric that reflects how a user’s body is tracking relative to their chronological age. Users can also incorporate clinical laboratory data, such as A1c and LDL cholesterol, to enrich their long-term health picture.”

At-home movement evaluations: “make physical assessments accessible without requiring specialized equipment. Using an iPhone camera and Apple Watch, users can measure their flexibility, strength, balance, movement mechanics, and VO2 max with real-time audio and visual feedback. Powered by on-device vision-based AI models and developed with clinical experts, the experience runs entirely on device; no video is ever recorded, stored, or shared.“

Additionally, Apple says that the new Health app offers expanded language support. It is available in global English, Chinese (Simplified and Traditional), French, Japanese, Korean, Norwegian, Portuguese, Spanish, Turkish, and Vietnamese.

#3501. Casey Anthony Helping YNW Melly's Legal Team Prepare for Double-Murder Retrial

Well, isn't this ironic ... Casey Anthony has been brought in to help rapper YNW Melly's legal team prepare for his upcoming double-murder retrial in January ... and it could be a smart move, because if there's anyone who knows about fighting murder charges in Florida, it's Casey.

Sources familiar with the case tell TMZ ... Casey is working as a research assistant for a private investigator named Pat McKenna, who was hired by a law firm representing Melly. Casey's a resource unlike any other -- she was at the center of one of the most controversial murder cases in American history.

We're told Casey is helping the attorneys research various aspects of the case as they prepare to defend the rapper when he heads back to court. Ya gotta figure they're picking Tot Mom's brain.

Melly is charged with two counts of first-degree murder in connection with the October 2018 killings of his close friends and fellow rappers Anthony Williams, known as YNW Sakchaser, and Christopher Thomas Jr., known as YNW Juvy.

Prosecutors allege Melly shot and killed both men inside a vehicle before he and his co-defendant, Cortlen Henry, known as YNW Bortlen, staged the crime scene to look like a drive-by shooting.

Melly's first trial ended in a mistrial in July 2023 after jurors failed to reach a unanimous verdict.

In September 2025, Henry pleaded no contest to accessory after the fact and received a 10-year prison sentence, followed by probation.

Melly has remained behind bars since his February 2019 arrest. His retrial is scheduled for January 2027 in Broward County.

TMZ reached out to Casey, Pat, Melly's lawyers, and his family members ... no word back.

Bringing in Casey to help Melly's defense is fascinating on a number of levels.

Casey became a household name in 2008 after the disappearance of her 2-year-old daughter, Caylee. Casey claimed her child was kidnapped by a babysitter ... but months later, she was arrested and charged with murder.

Casey's highly publicized trial in Florida gripped the nation, and in 2011, a jury acquitted her of murder, aggravated child abuse, and aggravated manslaughter.

She was convicted of four misdemeanor counts of providing false information to law enforcement, though two of those convictions were later overturned on appeal ... and the case remains one of the most polarizing trials in history.

This is like asking Tiger Woods to help with your golf swing.

#3500. Jason Momoa's 12-Part Crime Thriller Officially Finds a New Streaming Home

Before Jason Momoa became one of Hollywood's biggest action stars, he was actually just a journeyman television actor trying to find his big break. Now, while most audiences remember his early success in Game of Thrones, there's another television drama from the same period that never quite received the attention it deserved and now, more than a decade after its original premiere, the entire series has found another opportunity to reach audiences.

Momoa's forgotten crime thriller The Red Road has officially returned to Netflix in the United States, with both seasons joining the platform on November 1. The show, which originally aired on SundanceTV between 2014 and 2015, was created by Aaron Guzikowski (Prisoners) and it studies the increasingly dangerous relationship between a small-town police officer and a member of a neighboring Native American community.

The series revolves around a local sheriff struggling to keep his family together while simultaneously policing two clashing communities: the small town where he grew up just outside of New York City, and the neighboring mountains — home of a federally unrecognized Native American tribe. After a terrible tragedy and cover-up further divides these worlds, an uneasy alliance is forged between the officer and a dangerous member of the tribe. As each of the two men find themselves increasingly compromised by the other and the emotional ghosts of their collective pasts begin to emerge, the lives of both quickly unravel, leading to terrible consequences.

Season 2 sees every character face an ordeal: Jean learns of dark family secrets, Kopus battles his conscience, and Harold must decide where his morals lie, but the question is, can any of them find their redemption before it all comes to an end?

The cast stars Jason Momoa (Aquaman) as Phillip Kopus, Martin Henderson (Virgin River) as Harold Jensen, Julianne Nicholson (Mare of Easttown) as Jean Jensen, Tamara Tunie (Law & Order: Special Victims Unit) as Marie Van Der Veen, Annalise Basso (Snowpiercer) as Kate Jensen, Allie Gonino (The Lying Game) as Rachel Jensen, Kiowa Gordon (The Twilight Saga: Eclipse) as Junior Van Der Veen, and Lisa Bonet (The Cosby Show) as Sky Van Der Veen.

The series ran for two seasons and 12 episodes before SundanceTV canceled it in 2015. It previously left Netflix in June 2026, making its November return particularly welcome for viewers who missed the opportunity to watch it earlier in the year.

Both seasons of The Red Road are streaming now on Netflix in the United States.

#3498. iOS 27.3 and macOS 27.3 add Vertical Tabs, Adaptive Dark Mode, and more to Safari

Apple just released the first betas of iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3, with some big changes to Safari. The updates add a new vertical tab layout, Adaptive Dark Mode, and Siri AI Custom Actions.

Safari in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3 is adding a new Vertical Tabs design option. If you choose this design, you’ll see your tabs arranged vertically along the left-hand side of Safari rather than along the top, as in the traditional Safari design.

By default, Vertical Tabs show as icons in order to maximize vertical and horizontal space. If you’d like, you can also resize the tab bar to see website titles.

To try Vertical Tabs in the new iOS 27.3 beta, head to the Settings app, choose Apps, tap Safari, then look for the new Vertical Tabs option. On Mac and iPad, the feature can also be enabled via the “View” menu in the Safari app directly.

Vertical tab layouts have become an increasingly popular web browser feature. Arc from The Browser Company popularized the option. Arc, however, ceased development last year, and The Browser Company announced last month that it will discontinue it altogether in December.

If you regularly visit a website that doesn’t support Dark Mode, Apple’s next round of software updates adds Adaptive Dark Mode. This will automatically apply Dark Mode to websites that don’t support the feature.

If Dark Mode is enabled on your iPhone, iPad, or Mac and you visit a website that doesn’t support it, you’ll see a new “Try” button. If you tap this, Safari will automatically create a Dark Mode version of the website.

You can choose to have Adaptive Dark Mode automatically kick in or use it on a site-by-site basis.

Finally, Siri AI can now take direct action on tabs in iOS 27.3, iPadOS 27.3, and macOS 27.3. This includes things like using Siri to move, sort, organize, and close your tabs.

In a future update, Siri’s on-screen awareness will also expand to include the entire content of a website, not just what’s visible on the screen at a particular moment.

iOS 27.3, macOS 27.3, and iPadOS 27.3 are rolling out to developers for beta testing today. The update will likely be released to everyone sometime in December. What do you think of these new Safari features? Will you try out the new Vertical Tabs feature? Let us know down in the comments.

#3494. watchOS 27.3 beta adds new Siri Recap and Live Rewind features for Apple Watch

Apple has released the first beta of watchOS 27.3 for developers, including two new Audio Intelligence features for Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4: Siri Recap and Live Rewind.

Apple first announced these features at its special event in September, saying they would “arrive in beta later this year.”

As a refresher, Siri Recap creates high-level summaries of conversations that you can review later. When the feature is enabled, Apple Intelligence will automatically generate a title and key points that you can review in the Siri app on iPhone.

Siri Recap ambiently takes notes on your conversations throughout your day and creates high-level Apple Intelligence–generated summaries that you can use later to jog your memory, so you can stay present in the moment. Your summaries auto-delete after 7 days if you choose not to save them.

You can turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone. When you enable it, you can set a schedule based on time and/or location, or you can manually turn it on or off. You can also access it via Control Center on Apple Watch.

Live Rewind, meanwhile, helps you recall what was just said in a conversation. You can activate Live Rewind by double-pressing the Digital Crown, and then see a transcript of the previous 15 seconds of a conversation.

Live Rewind recalls what was just said in the last 15 seconds by showing a text snippet on your Apple Watch when you double-press the Digital Crown, so you can catch something you missed or are less familiar with. You can ask Siri about the content of the snippet or simply save it to the Siri app.

Siri Recap’s summary is described as a “brief, high-level summary of conversations,” not a transcript. Apple says it will “exclude sensitive information like financial information or government-assigned identifiers.”

Live Rewind text snippets and Siri Recap summaries are end-to-end encrypted. Apple says the features “do not create or store audio recordings, and raw audio used for processing is completely inaccessible to the operating systems, apps, the user, or Apple.” The company uses the S11 chip’s Secure Exclave to power the features, a “dedicated hardware-isolated compartment that processes audio in complete isolation from the rest of the system, then immediately deletes it.”

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are available in beta with watchOS 27.3, which is available now for developers.

A price drop always stands out more when the product in question already has a reputation for delivering above its size, and that’s the case with the Bose SoundLink Plus. It hasn’t been on the market for long, but it’s already earned strong reviews—CNET labeled it “the Goldilocks of Bose Bluetooth speakers.” And right now, ahead of Black Friday, it’s down to $179 from $269, which price trackers show is the lowest it’s ever been.

Bose positions it right in the middle of the SoundLink lineup, and you feel that balance in how it’s built. #3487. iOS 27.3 introduces new iPhone Duo feature for one-handed use

iOS 27.3 beta 1 launched today with a variety of new features, including a big upgrade for one-handed iPhone Duo use thanks to Reachability.

When iPhone Duo reviews first arrived last month, some complained that the extra-wide design of the outer display made it difficult to use one-handed.

At the time, Apple said that it would introduce Reachability via a future software update to help.

Today with iOS 27.3 beta 1, Reachability has officially arrived for iPhone Duo users.

Unlike Reachability on other iPhones, which shifts the screen down vertically, the iPhone Duo version works horizontally.

Once the feature is enabled (Settings ⇾ Accessibility ⇾ Reachability), a short swipe to the side of the screen will shift everything to the left or right, making it easier to reach.

If you’re struggling at all with one-handed iPhone Duo use, iOS 27.3 might make a big difference.

Currently iOS 27.3 is only available in developer beta, but a public beta is expected to launch in the coming days. However, if you’re concerned about bugs or performance issues, we recommend waiting for the launch version. Apple has said that iOS 27.3 will ship to all users next month, with mid-December the most likely window.

Have you tried Reachability on iPhone Duo yet? How is it working for you? Let us know in the comments.

#3486. Eight 'Winter Arc' Rules That Will Actually Deliver Results

There are a lot of terrible social media trends out there aimed at self-improvement, yet even though everybody has been making fun of the "Winter Arc" craze, I actually think it’s a good one. During your Winter Arc, you promise yourself you’ll stick to your fitness and self-care routines during (and despite) the end-of-year chaos. It's a good goal, with one caveat: Make sure you choose rules that will actually improve your life and deliver results.

Think of the “arc” in the sense of a “story arc.” The Winter Arc is a self-improvement journey that unfolds over the last few months of the calendar year. The most hardcore #gymtok-ers will tell you the Winter Arc officially begins on Oct. 1, but others start in early November, or whenever they get around to it. The "when" isn't critical, though—whenever you read this is a fine time to start. The close of the Winter Arc is fixed, however: It ends Jan. 1, just as everybody who is less dedicated than you is waking from their holiday food comas and resolving to get in shape.

You get to choose your own terms for your Winter Arc. The general vibe is one of locking in, committing to your goals, and actually doing the things you’re always saying you’ll do. TikToker @carlyupgraded has said that her own mental image of someone nailing their Winter Arc is “hood up, headphones on, getting ready to go for a run in the rain at 5 a.m.”

It turns out I’ve accidentally been Winter-Arc-ing for years; I just didn’t know it had a catchy name. Why save your gym routine for New Year’s when you’ll have the place to yourself all December? We’re even gifted with an extra hour in the mornings to fill with something productive.

I really love the mindset shift involved. Commonly, people are active in the summer (great time for outdoor fun), may or may not stick with their routines in the fall, and let everything fall apart as the holidays approach. Who has time to go to the gym when you’re planning Thanksgiving, attending holiday parties, studying for final exams, or whatever else the end of the year throws in front of you?

But that’s the exact reason why this time of year is the best to start (or restart) a fitness routine, or really any kind of routine. When you start a routine during a busy time of year, you’ll be forced to make it sustainable. The gym routine you can stick with amid the chaos isn’t going to be one you drop after a few months. You’re already training yourself to work around obstacles as they come up, which is a key component of self-efficacy. And when the chaos clears on Jan. 1, your routine will be even easier to stick to.

Of course, there are ways to lean in too hard: Choosing unsustainable habits, falling for bad diet advice, mistaking not masturbating for some kind of health hack, the usual suspects. There’s also the pitfall of focusing too much on the vibes and too little on what you’re actually going to do or how you’ll benefit.

And then there’s the framing: You were working on yourself all year, but you’re in danger of letting up on the gas, but you’re committed to locking in so that you’re a step ahead of everybody who takes this time to slack off. I really don’t love this tack. Self-improvement is not a competition. There’s a difference between being consistent in your training and healthy eating (good) and seeing the pursuit of health and fitness as something where you always have to work harder because you’re at risk of getting left behind.

I also don’t love how gendered the Winter Arc TikToks tend to be. When you search for Winter Arc content, the first few suggestions include “winter arc for women” and “winter arc for men.” When I first started looking at the Winter Arc trend a few years ago, the women’s versions were more likely to include restrictive dieting or to focus on how the Winter Arc will finally (sigh) snatch your waist. These days, the focus is more on personal goal setting: Lots of the girlies filming their Winter Arc rules are doing so in a notebook and talking about journaling exercises that will help you identify what you need to work on to get to your "best self." Sometimes this is all monetized; training plans and journaling prompts can, of course, be purchased at the link in bio.

I do like that many of the women’s versions emphasize sustainability and setting your own goals rather than copying somebody else's. I don't love the enormity of the mental burden you're supposed to shoulder before even beginning. Should I really have to file an in-depth written report with myself before revamping every area of my life with a 100% commitment to multiple goals?

The men’s versions tend to go off the rails in another direction, with rules like “no girls” or “go ghost.” No distractions! Here, I've seen a shift over the years as well: at first there was overly serious content, followed quickly by satire (yelling at the viewer to get divorced and go work out in the dark). Now the men's videos tend to be more vibes-based, featuring images of pre-dawn workouts and plates full of salad with motivational quotes playing in the background. When the men give their rules, they tend to be simpler than the women's—no journaling exercises—but they often boil down to the same overly strict routines. (And then, of course, they'll offer to sell you a 90-day or 60-day plan.)

If you’re going to do a Winter Arc (or if you’re already doing one), make sure to structure it in a way that benefits you. Choosing 10 overly ambitious goals and setting yourself up for failure is not a healthy way to approach self-improvement, OK? Pick goals that are meaningful, achievable without divine intervention, and trackable with tools you already have at hand (for example, tracking your steps with a Fitbit or your running mileage with a Garmin watch).

It’s also helpful to think of developing yourself over this arc, rather than taking it as a three-month (or two-month) challenge where you have to do everything right all the time. If you currently wake up at 8 a.m. and want to wake up at 5 a.m., you don’t have to set your alarm for 5 a.m. tomorrow. It’s OK to aim for 7:30 a.m., make that a habit, then try for 7:00 a.m., and so on.

With that in mind, here are some "rules" I've seen from creators that I'm actually on board with (so long as you don't overwhelm yourself with them):

Wake up earlier. A great goal, especially if you take advantage of the time change to make things easier on your body.

Get to bed on time. Never a bad idea. Cultivating good sleep habits in general is always worthwhile.

Get your steps in. Be thoughtful about what your target is: 10,000 is not for everybody. Better to choose a number that would be a modest improvement on what you already do.

Exercise X times per week. Pick a number that works for you, and get into it. Be realistic about your goal, and for the best results, be consistent even if you’re sore at first.

Eat healthy. This is a great goal, with the major caveat that there are a lot of ways to eat healthy. You don’t need to cut out sugar or pretend that there’s something evil about seed oils. Do get more protein and veggies.

Be more thoughtful about using social media. I’m not going to tell you to delete all your apps (“except TikTok,” as the TikTokers say). But it’s fair to consider whether you might want to delete a few apps, turn off some notifications, or put your phone on Do Not Disturb for more hours of the day.

Journal or read more. Journaling can be great for working through your feelings or cultivating a creative habit. Reading can be entertainment or a great way to learn. Choose whichever you need most.

Learn a new skill. I’ve mostly seen this one in the men’s TikToks, and I love it. They’re often thinking of “skills” that will help in some kind of entrepreneurship grift they’re about to sell you, but there are tons of skills that will come in handy in life, or that are at least fun to learn. Practice a language, get better at cooking, make some art. Skills are, as I’ve noted, a multi-layered exercise for your brain. And they may come in handy someday.

This year I've slacked off on my fitness routine as I've gotten more involved in other hobbies, but I'm actually looking forward to being more consistent. My winter goals include exercising early in the day when possible and reading 20 minutes each day. (I'm even tracking the second one with a sticker chart.)

#3485. iOS 27.3 expands Siri AI with many new capabilities across Apple apps

iOS 27.3 has just entered beta testing and includes major new features for Siri AI across iPhone, iPad and Mac. The company has unlocked many new capabilities across major Apple apps, like Music, Messages, Safari, Reminders and more.

We are still digging into the beta, but here’s a taste of what new things you can get Siri AI to do:

With the Music app, you can now create playlists and save them to your library, like you can ask it to make you “a playlist for songs for a day at the beach”, and then save it for later.

In Messages, you can now ask it to schedule iMessages to be sent later, edit and unsent messages, as well as respond with emoji reactions. You can compose new Notes with bold, italic, and rich text formatting, organize your Notes folders, and more.

Photos gets a big expansion with new Siri AI capabilities that let you favorite photos, rotate and edit images, and rename people and pets all with your voice.

You can now use Siri AI with the Calendar app to create events featuring invitees, location, video call links and more. And in Reminders, you can now create urgent reminders for the first time with Siri.

In Safari, you can now use Siri to create tap groups from a list of URLs, sort your tabs, clear your history, delete reading list items and more.

Journal support with Siri AI is new for the first time. You can create entries with text transcription, or record audio entries.

There’s also wide support for file and folder management with Siri AI Files integration. You can get file content, create files and folders, send files to the trash, organize by type, rename files, and more, using just your voice.

We are also seeing new Siri features for Weather, Maps, Preview and Shortcuts, and will keep testing to find new integrations. Apple is also opening up this support to third-party developers.

iOS 27.3 is currently in beta testing and will be released publicly later this year.

And while the property continues searching for a renter, D4vd's legal troubles have only piled up.

D4vd has pleaded not guilty to the criminal charges.

#3481. Developers can now create advanced ‘app skills’ for Siri AI

Apple today announced a major new Siri AI initiative for third-party developers, allowing any app to create Siri AI integrations for the first time. The first versions of Siri AI were limited to a much smaller set of supported schemas.

The new ‘app skills’ also let apps teach Siri how to coordinate complicated multi-step actions. These features are testable in the iOS 27.3 betas.

The app skills sound very similar to what other LLM-driven AI models offer, enabling richer understanding of complicated tasks.

For example, a flight tracking app skill will be able to cleanly map what app intents Siri should use to service a particular kind of user request; something that the first version of Siri AI was simply incapable of doing.

Of course, Apple itself has also taken advantage of the new Siri AI foundational features, with a significant rollout of new capabilities across Apple’s apps.

Here’s an example of what Siri will be able to do, from the developer documentation:

Siri can find custom content from one app, transfer it to a specified app, and perform an action. For example, somebody might request “Hey Siri, send my favorite sneakers to my partner in name of a messaging app.” Siri finds sneakers that the person added to their favorites, understands who the partner is, finds them in Contacts, then sends the sneaker information to them using the messaging app.

It’s also going to be a lot easier to initiate Siri actions for third-party apps. With the Siri AI Developer Preview, users don’t have to explicitly mention the app’s name in many circumstances. For instance, if a Live Activity for a ride-sharing app is active, Siri will automatically understand that a request to “change the ride address” corresponds to the app driving the Live activity.

This gives you a sense of the kinds of things Siri will be able to do in the future, coordinating more complicated actions across Apple and third-party apps.

The new OS releases are in developer beta right now, but Apple says the app skills support is only an early developer preview and is scheduled to officially roll out in the spring.

#3477. Trump Launches Triumphal Arch Website Right As Judge Blocks Construction

After his party suffered a brutal loss in the 2026 midterms, Donald Trump has tried to find solace in his attempts to remake Washington, D.C. But thanks to one federal judge, Trump is beginning to learn that exerting his will over the forces of state bureaucracy may not be as easy as it once was.

Late on Thursday, Judge Tanya Chutkan of the District of Columbia brought one of Trump’s prize beautification projects to a screeching halt, ruling that construction on Trump’s triumphal arch must be stopped pending the outcome of a combined legal case that names both Trump himself and the federal National Parks Service as defendants. The timing of Chutkan’s ruling couldn’t have been worse: As it came down, the White House was in the process of rolling out a glossy new website for the project, featuring 3D renderings and sweeping views of a grand structure that now may never actually be built.

A Monument to the American Spirit.The Military Triumphal Arch will honor the heroes who gave everything for our nation – a monumental tribute to America’s first 250 years & a symbol of the next 250.A legacy of freedom. A future without limits.📲 https://t.co/vkquwA5qGp pic.twitter.com/ucUPdw3YLL

This is not Chutkan’s first run-in with Trump or his administration. In 2023, Chutkan oversaw the criminal trial against Trump for his attempt to overturn the 2020 election, a case that was only dismissed after Trump won the presidency in 2024, on the basis that the federal government could not prosecute sitting presidents.

But she hasn’t been an unequivocal Trump opponent. The following year, in 2025, Chutkan declined to block the so-called Department of Government Efficiency from accessing federal employee data, saying that the plaintiffs trying to block DOGE’s power failed to prove the agency would cause “immediate, irreparable harm.”

On this ruling, however, she did not find any merit to what the government was arguing — and her opinion was unsparing on that count.

“Defendants also assert — belatedly — that the Arch represents ‘a generational national defense opportunity,’ and that the Arch may assist in combating or deterring assassination attempts on the President,” Chutkan wrote in her ruling. “The court appreciates the government’s significant interest in national security. But these recent and unsupported attestations of security … appear nowhere in the planning documents on which the project was reviewed and approved. Indeed, they materialized, for the first time, when Defendants filed their opposition brief last week.” Editor’s picks The 250 Greatest Albums of the 21st Century So Far The 100 Best TV Episodes of All Time The 500 Greatest Albums of All Time 100 Best Movies of the 21st Century

In less-legal terms, Chutkan is basically noting that, as opponents of the arch have suggested for months, Trump and his cronies made up some utter flimflam about the “security” opportunities of an enormous arch in the middle of D.C. and tried to shoehorn it through legal review. Chutkan has said in no uncertain terms that that’s not going to cut it.

“The White House commends the National Capital Planning Commission’s decision to fully approve President Trump’s historic vision to build a much-needed Triumphal Arch in Washington, D.C.,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle posted after the ruling. “An activist district court thereafter blocked the construction of the project.”

The judge’s posture toward the flimsy legal work of the Trump administration mirrors that of another federal judge, Ana C. Reyes, who exploded at administration lawyers in court a few weeks back after they tried to pull a fast one on her during Trump’s renovation of the East Potomac Golf Links. Reyes’ beef with the administration was more explicit — she accused them of explicitly betraying her trust — but similar to the core of Chutkan’s argument here. #3469. Your Android Can Get Hacked Without You Doing Anything at All

You probably know that clicking suspicious links online or opening attachments from strangers in an email or text is a recipe for hacking. It's a dangerous world out there online, so it's always important to be vigilant. However, the danger doesn't always involve something you do. There are ways to hack your devices without requiring any intervention on your part whatsoever—and one such example is likely plaguing your Android device right now.

As reported by The Hacker News, there is a critical Android security flaw that could enable remote code execution on your device. In other words, bad actors could use the flaw to run their own code on your phone, effectively taking over the device for their own gain. The flaw, identified as CVE-2026-58868, isn't universal, but it is widespread: It currently affects Android 14 through Android 17, the latest version of Google's OS. If your phone runs Android 12 or Android 13, it may be unaffected, as Google doesn't identify these versions in its security bulletin, but it doesn't explicitly rule them out, either.

There are two silver linings here, however. One, Google hasn't confirmed any active exploits for this security flaw. While that isn't a guarantee that bad actors have missed this exploit so far, it at least opens that possibility. As such, there may be time for users to patch their devices before hackers truly take advantage of the flaw. Second, Google does have a patch for the flaw. The patch may not be available to you right away, however, as it's up to both the manufacturer of your phone and your carrier to issue these updates. Still, a patch is, at the very least, on its way.

This flaw is perhaps the most important to fix, but it's not the only serious issue. In all, Google's latest bulletin highlights 216 vulnerabilities, and, of those, 23 are "critical." As The Hacker News explains, two other of those critical flaws could also allow remote code execution when exploited.

To see whether the patch is installed on your end, open the Settings app on your phone, tap "About phone" or "About tablet," then choose the Android version on-screen. Look for a date of "2026-11-01" or later. All security patches from Nov. 1 and on will fix this issue. If not, you'll ned to wait for the patch.

#3468. iOS 27.3 brings the iPhone Duo’s revamped StandBy to other iPhones

Apple released iOS 27.3 beta 1 today, with a surprisingly extensive set of new features and improvements across the system. One of them is the expansion of the iPhone Duo’s redesigned StandBy experience to other iPhone models. Here are the details.

When Apple announced the iPhone Duo, one of its exclusive new features was a redesigned StandBy experience with new clock faces and expanded customization options.

StandBy mode was introduced with iOS 17, and it essentially turns the iPhone into a smart display when placed horizontally while charging.

Until now, users of other iPhone models were limited to the original StandBy experience, which offered clock, widget, and photo views, but lacked the additional faces and more extensive customization options introduced with the iPhone Duo.

With iOS 27.3, however, Apple is extending the redesigned Analog and Digital Clock faces to other iPhones, with additional options for customizing their colors and complications. In addition to the new Calendar and Weather faces, the update adds support for Shared Albums to the Photos face, letting users choose which shared photos appear in StandBy.

Users with an iPhone 11 or later can now also create multiple versions of the same StandBy face, each with its own customization options, and swipe between them.

iOS 27.3 is expected to launch in December. To learn more about StandBy and how to customize its different faces, follow this link.
